title: White Fang

subtitle.text: Tall dark spruce trees lined the frozen waterway. The land was silent and empty.
So cold, so lonely, it seemed impossible for anything to survive. This was the Wild, the savage, frozen land of the North.
But there was life in this land. A line of dogs made their way along the frozen waterway.
Their breath froze in the air, forming into crystals of frost and settling on their fur. The dogs wore leather harnesses that were attached to a sled.
The sled held several items—blankets, an ax, a coffeepot, a frying pan. But most of the sled's space was taken up by a long and narrow box.
A man wearing wide snowshoes blazed a trail ahead of the dogs as a second man worked at the rear of the sled.
The box on the sled held a third man whose work was over—a man whom the Wild had conquered.
But the two men working the sled were not yet conquered.
Their bodies were covered with fur and leather.
Their eyelashes and cheeks and lips were so coated with the crystals from their frozen breath that they appeared to be ghosts.
But under it all, they were alive, battling this frozen, unwelcoming world. The two men traveled without speech, saving their breath for the work of their bodies.
The pale light of the short day was just fading when a faint cry came from far away.
The front man turned his head until his eyes met the eyes of the man behind. Across the narrow coffin, they nodded to each other.
More fierce, hungry cries came. Both men knew where the sounds were coming from—the snowy land that they had just left behind.
"They're after us, Bill," said the man at the front. His voice was hoarse.
"Meat is scarce," Bill answered. "They're hungry."
They spoke no more, but listened carefully as the animals' hunting cries continued to rise behind them.
When darkness fell, the men found a cluster of spruce trees and made a camp.
They used the coffin, lying by the fire, for both seats and a table. The sled dogs snarled and bickered among themselves.
"Seems to me, Henry, the dogs are staying pretty close to camp," Bill said.
Henry nodded and set the coffeepot on the fire. "They know where it's safe."
"Did you notice the way the dogs got upset when I was feeding them?" Bill asked.
"They did go wild more than usual," Henry agreed.
Bill ate some beans. "How many dogs do we have, Henry?"
"Six."
"That's true," Bill said.
"We've got six dogs with us. I took six fish out of the bag, and I gave one fish to each dog."
He paused to make sure Henry wouldn't miss what he had to say next. "But I was one fish short."
"You counted wrong," Henry said.
"I counted right," Bill replied. "I took out six fish. But there were seven dogs waiting for food. By the time I got to One Ear, I was all out of fish."
Henry stopped eating to glance across the fire and count the dogs. "There are only six dogs now."
Bill nodded. "I saw the seventh one run off across the snow."
Henry sighed. "I'll be mighty glad when this trip's over."
"Why?" Bill asked.
"You're starting to see things."
"I thought you'd say that," Bill answered.
"And so I went and looked in the snow. I saw the tracks."
Henry took a swig of coffee. "So you're thinking it was—"
A long howl broke through the cold air. The two men listened, and then Henry waved his hand toward the sound.
"You think it was one of those wolves?"
Bill nodded. "It would explain why our sled dogs went wild at feeding time."
More hungry cries sounded in the distance. The dogs huddled closer to the fire as Bill threw on more firewood. Then he sat down again.
"I'll tell you something, Henry." Bill tapped the box they were sitting on.
"The fellow in here is much luckier than you or I. Why, if we die out here in the Wild, nobody's going to pay for a funeral for us."
"Nope," Henry agreed. "We don't have loads of money like he had."
"Here's what I don't understand," Bill said.
"Why would a rich chap like this, who's a lord in his own country, ever come out to a godforsaken place like this?"
"He might have lived to a ripe old age if he'd stayed home," Henry replied.
Bill opened his mouth to speak, but instead he pointed. A pair of gleaming eyes had appeared in the darkness.
Henry indicated with his head a second pair, and a third pair of eyes. A circle of eyes now surrounded their camp.
The sled dogs crawled closer to the two men.
Bill shook his head. "It's a shame we're so low on ammunition."
"How much is left?" Henry asked.
"Three cartridges," Bill answered. "And I wish it was three hundred." He glanced at the glowing eyes.
"I wish this trip was over, and you and I were sitting by the fire in Fort McGurry, playing cards."
Henry nodded.
Before long the two men were asleep. As the fire died down, the glowing eyes crept closer.
The sled dogs snarled and barked, waking up Bill. He got up and threw more wood on the fire to keep the wolves back.
Bill glanced at the sled dogs. He rubbed his eyes, and then looked at them more sharply.
"Henry," he said.
Henry groaned. "What's wrong now?"
"I just counted the dogs again. There are seven now!"
"Huh?" Henry just grunted and drifted back into sleep. Uneasily, Bill fell back to sleep too.
The two men got up at six o'clock. But daylight in the North was still three hours away, so it was still dark.
Henry prepared breakfast while Bill rolled the blankets and got the sled ready for lashing.
"Say, Henry," Bill said suddenly. "How many dogs did you say we had?"
"Six."
"Well, you're wrong," Bill said.
"Seven again?" Henry asked.
"No, five. One's gone."
"What?" Henry ran over to count the dogs. "You're right, Bill. Fatty's gone."
"The wolves must have gotten him." Bill shook his head. "He always was a fool dog."
"But even a fool dog should know better than to leave the camp."
Henry looked over the rest of the sled dogs. "I bet none of the others would do it."
"Yep," Bill agreed. "I always did think there was something wrong with Fatty."
With breakfast eaten, and the dogs harnessed to the sled, the two men headed into the darkness.
They continued their slow, exhausting trek toward Fort McGurry.
Daylight finally came at nine o'clock. At midday the sky to the south turned pink, but that color swiftly faded.
By three o'clock, the full Arctic night had descended upon the silent land again. As darkness came on, so did the hunting cries.
A few hours later, Bill and Henry stopped for the day, to make camp.
Henry was tending a pot of beans when he heard a shout from Bill, and a snarling cry of pain.
Henry looked up, and saw a dim shape disappear into the darkness.
Bill stood amid the dogs, holding a club in one hand and part of a dried salmon in the other.
"It got half of the salmon," Bill announced. "But I got a whack at it. Did you hear it squeal?"
Henry nodded. "What did it look like?"
"It looked like any of our sled dogs," Bill said. "I reckon it's a tame wolf."
"It must be tame, coming here at feeding time," Henry agreed.
When supper was finished, they sat on the coffin.
Henry stared at the fire while Bill watched the circle of eyes that burned in the darkness just beyond the firelight.
"I wish they'd catch a moose or something and leave us alone," Bill murmured.
Henry grunted. "We'll reach Fort McGurry soon enough."
In the morning Henry was awakened by a shout from Bill.
"What's wrong?" Henry called.
"Frog's gone," Bill answered.
"No."
"Yes!"
Henry pushed away the blankets and ran to the dogs. He counted them and then sighed.
"Frog was the strongest dog of the bunch," Bill said.
"And he was no fool." Henry shook his head. "I'm sure the wolves got him."
That night Bill carefully tied the dogs to stakes set firmly in the ground.
Henry nodded his approval. "They can't run off now."
Bill folded his arms. "If any of these dogs are missing in the morning, I'll go without my coffee."
Later the men watched as glowing eyes appeared again in the darkness.
One of the sled dogs began to whine, pulling and biting furiously at its stake.
"One Ear is trying to get loose," Henry whispered.
"Look over there!" Bill pointed.
A doglike animal glided past the firelight, its attention on the dogs.
"It's a she-wolf!" Henry whispered. "She must act as a decoy for the pack. She gets a male dog to follow her, and then the pack jumps in and eats him!"
The men's eyes followed the animal as it disappeared from sight.
"A wolf that knows to come in with the dogs at feeding time has been around people," Henry said.
Bill nodded. "A friend of mine once had a dog that ran away. We saw that dog three years later, running with a pack of wolves."
"I reckon you've solved the mystery, Bill," Henry said. "That wolf is no wolf—it's a dog."
"Dog or not, we can't afford to lose any more of our animals," Bill said flatly. "First chance I get, I'm going to put an end to that beast."
"But you've only got three cartridges," Henry reminded him.
"I'll wait for a good shot."
In the morning Henry was up first. When Bill sat down to breakfast, he reached for the coffeepot.
"You don't get any coffee," Henry told him.
"We didn't run out, did we?" Bill asked anxiously.
"Nope."
Irritation showed in Bill's face. "Then explain why I don't get any."
"Spanker's gone," Henry answered.
"No! How'd it happen?"
Henry shrugged. "Don't know." Then he held out the coffeepot. "Go ahead, Bill. Have some coffee."
Bill shook his head. "I said I wouldn't have any coffee if a dog went missing, and I won't!"
"It's darn good coffee," Henry coaxed him.
But Bill was stubborn, and took none of it. A quarter of an hour later, the men broke camp.
Bill started loading the sled. "I have a bad feeling."
"You'll feel better when we pull into Fort McGurry," Henry replied.
"Half our dogs are gone," Bill muttered. "It won't be long before those wolves set their eyes on us."
Henry laughed. "I've never been trailed by wolves before, but I've gone through worse things and kept my health."
The two men set out in silence. Around noon Bill reached for the rifle. "You keep going, Henry. I'm going to see what I can see."
"You should stick by the sled," Henry protested. "You've only got three cartridges."
"Who's worried now?" Bill said with a chuckle.
Henry plodded on alone, casting back anxious glances every few minutes. An hour later Bill caught up with the sled.
"The wolves are hunting for game now," he reported. "But they're still following us. They're pretty thin, Henry.
Their ribs are like washboards, and their stomachs are right up against their backbones. I tell you, those wolves are hungry."
A few minutes later, Henry noticed a furry, slinking shape trotting silently behind the sled. He whistled for Bill to stop.
"It's the she-wolf," Bill said.
The animal was just a hundred yards away.
It looked at the men in a strangely wistful way, almost as a dog would. But there was no affection in this animal's gaze. There was only a cruel hunger.
Bill shouted and waved his hands threateningly, but the she-wolf showed no fear.
He then reached for the gun again. As he brought it to his shoulder, the she-wolf leaped sideways from the trail and disappeared.
Henry let out a long whistle.
Bill shook his head as he put the gun away.
"That wolf knows about guns too! I'm going to have to sneak up on that critter if I want to kill it. And I will, as sure as my name is Bill."
"You just be careful," his partner warned. "If that pack manages to surround you, those three cartridges won't do you any good."
They camped early that night. Three dogs couldn't do the work of six, and their travel had become much slower.
The wolves were growing bolder, and Bill had to wake up several times to keep the fire raging. The fire kept the wolves at a safe distance.
"They're going to get us," Bill remarked as he crawled back under the blankets.
"A man is half dead when he thinks like that," Henry retorted sharply. He closed his eyes and rolled over, trying to get back to sleep.
Bill had sounded so gloomy. Henry would work on cheering him up tomorrow.
The men woke up the next morning to find that they'd lost no dogs during the night.
As they headed out onto the trail, their spirits were brighter. Bill seemed to have forgotten his uneasiness from the previous night.
Then, at midday, they overturned the sled on a rough part of the trail. The sled was upside down, jammed between a tree trunk and a huge rock.
The men unharnessed the dogs in order to turn over the sled. Right away One Ear moved away from them.
"Hey! One Ear!" Bill cried. "Get back here!"
But One Ear broke into a run back down the trail, where the she-wolf was waiting for him.
She moved playfully toward the dog, and then halted. The men called for One Ear to return again, but the dog ignored them.
When One Ear tried to sniff noses with the she-wolf, she retreated coyly.
One Ear advanced again. The she-wolf sniffed his nose briefly, and then retreated. Step-by-step, she was luring the dog away.
Bill reached for the rifle, but it was jammed beneath the overturned sled.
By the time he and Henry had set the sled right, One Ear and the she-wolf were too far away to risk a shot.
Suddenly One Ear turned and dashed back toward the sled. A dozen wolves, lean and gray, were approaching the trail!
The she-wolf's playfulness was gone. With a snarl she sprang after One Ear.
The dog left the trail, attempting to circle back to the sled, but the wolves kept coming. They were going to cut him off before he reached the sled.
"They're not getting any more of our dogs!" Bill declared.
Gun in hand, he plunged into the underbrush alongside the trail, moving toward the commotion.
"Be careful!" Henry called after him.
Bill was gone from sight, but Henry saw One Ear appear and disappear among the underbrush and scattered clumps of spruce.
He knew the poor dog's case was hopeless.
And then it happened.
Bang
! Henry heard a shot, rapidly followed by two more shots. "Oh no," he thought with dread. "Bill's ammunition is
gone." There were snarls and yelps, followed by the wolf cry that announces fallen prey. And then silence settled down again over the lonely
land. Henry sank onto the sled. There was no need for him to go and see what had happened. He knew it as though it had taken place before his
eyes. He sat brooding about his poor partner for a long while. Then wearily, he stood up, and fastened the two remaining dogs to the
sled. Henry continued on through the Wild toward the fort. At the first hint of darkness, he set up camp, making sure he had a generous supply of
firewood. He fed the sled dogs, ate his supper, and made his bed close to the
fire. The wolves soon returned. Henry spent a sleepless night keeping the fire ablaze, his only means of protection from the hungry
fangs. When the wolves approached too closely, Henry seized chunks of burning wood from the fire and hurled them into the
pack. The wolves backed away, snarling angrily and
yelping. By morning Henry was exhausted. He knew that his only chance for survival was to reach Fort McGurry as soon as possible.
He chopped down some young saplings and tied them high in a tree, so that they formed a scaffold.
Using ropes from the sled, he hoisted the coffin onto the scaffold. This would keep it safe from the wolves.
With a lighter sled, Henry hit the trail. But when the light of the sun dimmed a few hours later, he had to stop again.
Traveling at night was far too dangerous, and he needed the remaining light to chop firewood.
That night Henry had to work constantly to keep the wolves at bay. He tied a burning piece of wood to his right hand to keep himself from sleeping.
Each time his eyes started to close, the burn of the flame quickly awakened him.
He then threw burning wood at the wolves, fueled the fire again, and replaced the piece of wood on his hand.
This worked well for a while. But then the wood fell from his hand, and he soon drifted into a dream.
He was sitting in Fort McGurry, playing cards by the fire. From outside he heard howls.
The door burst open and wolves flooded into the room.
The howls grew louder and louder . . .
Suddenly Henry woke. "The sounds are real!" he thought.
Henry felt sharp teeth sink into his arm.
Instinctively he leaped into the fire, scooping up the burning wood and flinging it in every direction until the wolves backed away, yelping in pain.
Breathing heavily and badly burned, Henry shouted, "You haven't got me yet!"
He set to work, extending the fire into a large circle around himself.
His two dogs were nowhere to be seen, and it wasn't hard to imagine what had become of them.
Outside the fire circle, one of the wolves raised its head and howled, and the others soon joined the hunger cry.
By the time dawn came, the circle of fire had nearly died. The wolves drew closer.
One jumped in for an attack, missed, and landed on the hot coals with a cry.
Henry hurled more burning chunks of wood, but they were losing their effect.
The wolves leaped to avoid being hit, but they no longer ran away. By now the fire was nearly gone.
Defeated, Henry sat down and let his head fall forward. "Come in and get me," he mumbled. "I'm going to sleep."
His eyes closed for a moment, and when they opened, the she-wolf was standing directly in front of him. He felt his eyes close once more.
A moment later, though it seemed like hours to Henry, he awoke to find that a mysterious change had taken place.
The wolves were gone. The sounds of sled dogs barking and men shouting filled his ears.
Suddenly a man grabbed Henry's shoulder. "Where's Lord Alfred?"
Henry shook his head sleepily. "He's in a tree at the last camp."
"Dead?" the man shouted.
"Yes. In a box." Henry pushed the man away.
"Now leave me alone." His eyes closed once more. Two men eased him down upon the blankets, where he snored peacefully.
In the distance, the cries of the still hungry wolf pack cut though the frosty air.
It was the she-wolf who first heard the new men arriving. Right away she fled into the wilderness, abandoning the man in his circle of dying flames.
The remaining wolves eyed the man for a moment longer. Then they bounded off too, following the she-wolf's tracks in the snow.
Running at the front of the pack was a large gray wolf. He snarled angrily and snapped his fangs at any of the younger wolves who tried to pass him.
Before long the pack caught up to the she-wolf, who dropped in alongside the large wolf. He did not snarl at her, though, whenever she ran ahead of him.
In fact, it was she who threatened him if he ran too close to her. And when that happened, he showed no anger toward her.
On the she-wolf's other side ran an old, one-eyed wolf, grizzled and scarred.
He also felt the she-wolf's anger if he ran too close, and he also accepted it without complaint.
The two male wolves had no tolerance or kindness for each other. They often glanced at each other to growl and flash their sharp teeth.
Half-starved, the wolf pack ran across the frozen land. The wolves ran through the night and into the next day, searching desperately for food.
They crossed snowy ridges and a dozen ice-covered streams until finally they came upon an enormous bull moose.
Here was meat, and this time, their prey had no fire to protect it.
It was a brief fight, and fierce. The moose swung its antlers furiously and stomped its massive hooves.
But in the end, the big animal could not fight off such a large number of wolves. With their stomachs full, the wolves soon settled in to rest.
In the following days, they lived well, attacking the oldest and weakest members of the moose herds they came upon.
The famine was over.
Time went by, and the wolf pack began to split up.
Two by two, male and female, the wolves departed until only the she-wolf remained, along with the young leader and the old, one-eyed wolf.
The two males snarled and growled at each other, and their bickering soon turned violent. Fangs slashed as the two wolves collided, kicking up snow.
The she-wolf—the cause of it all—sat down contentedly and watched.
The younger wolf was strong, but the older one, with his lost eye and deep scars, had fought many battles.
When the younger wolf left himself vulnerable for a brief moment, the old wolf struck with his fangs.
He leaped in low and then quickly jumped away, leaving behind a terrible gash. The young wolf stumbled and fell, and then moved no more.
One Eye stalked over to the she-wolf and sniffed her nose.
The two wolves leaped about playfully, and then bounded off through the trees, running side by side, like good friends who have come to an understanding.
Days went by and the two wolves hunted and ate together.
The she-wolf often stopped to sniff around a cave or a crevice. She seemed in search of something, but what that thing was, One Eye did not know.
One moonlit night the she-wolf and One Eye ran through the quiet forest.
Suddenly One Eye caught a strange scent in the air, and halted. The scent worried him, but the she-wolf continued slowly toward it.
Nervously, One Eye followed. The sound of dogs fighting, along with the voices of men and women, soon came to his ears.
The wolves had reached an Indian camp, and while the smells and sounds were foreign to One Eye, the she-wolf knew them well.
One Eye sat uneasily next to his mate, watching the activity in the camp. Finally the she-wolf turned and trotted back into the forest, to the great relief of the old wolf.
As they moved along silently in the moonlight, they came upon a trail of fresh footprints in the snow.
One Eye followed them, and soon caught sight of a dim movement of white against the white of the snow—a snowshoe rabbit!
One Eye picked up speed, chasing the small animal between two rows of trees and into a clearing.
One Eye was about to pounce when something strange happened: the rabbit shot up into the air! There it hung, kicking wildly in a snare.
One Eye sprang back with fright, and then crouched, snarling threats at this thing of fear he did not understand.
But the she-wolf ran past him and sprang for the hanging rabbit.
She missed, and her teeth clipped emptily together with a snap. She made another leap, and another.
One Eye watched her curiously. Then, no longer scared, he too made a mighty spring upward.
His teeth closed upon the rabbit, and he pulled it back to earth with him.
But as he did so, he saw a young spruce sapling bending down above him, ready to strike.
His jaws let go of their grip, and he leaped backward to escape this strange danger.
And in that moment, the sapling stood back up, and the rabbit dangled in the air again.
The she-wolf was angry that he had lost the meal.
She sank her fangs into her mate's shoulder to punish him; and he, frightened and unaware of why she attacked, struck back.
Immediately he knew he'd made a mistake. She growled and bit him repeatedly, until he gave up any attempt to fight back.
In the meantime the rabbit still hung above them from the snare.
One Eye, now more scared of his mate than of the mysterious sapling, jumped for the rabbit again.
As he sank back with it between his teeth, he kept his eye on the thin tree. As before, it followed him downward.
With the rabbit still clamped in his jaws, he crouched down, expecting the sapling to strike him.
The sapling, however, did not attack, but remained bent over him. When he moved, the sapling moved.
And when he remained still, it too remained still. So he decided it was safer to remain still.
The she-wolf stepped over and ripped the rabbit from the snare. At once the sapling shot back up to its vertical position.
One Eye and his mate devoured the rabbit that the mysterious sapling had caught for them.
After that, the pair came across more rabbits hanging in the air, and through careful observation of his mate, One Eye learned the method of robbing snares.
For two days the she-wolf and One Eye stayed near the Indian camp, stealing prey from snares.
One morning a man appeared with a shiny stick that made a fierce sound.
Something smashed into a tree trunk inches from One Eye's head, and the two wolves raced back into the wilderness.
The she-wolf continued to sniff at crevices in rocks and other spots in the wild. Her need to find a particular thing soon seemed urgent.
She had grown heavy, and was running slowly.
When One Eye touched her neck gently with his muzzle, she snapped at him with such anger that he tumbled over backward.
Soon she found the thing she'd been looking for. It was a small cave along a frozen stream. She entered cautiously and came to a small chamber.
It was dry and warm. She inspected it with great care while One Eye stood in the entrance, patiently watching her.
Finally with her head toward the entrance, she lay down and curled up.
One Eye lay down in the entrance and slept too.
He kept waking up and cocking his ears at the bright world outside, where the April sun blazed across the snow, triggering faint whispers of trickling water.
The feel of spring was in the air—life was stirring.
One Eye cast anxious glances at his mate, but she showed no desire to leave her lair.
He looked outside, and several birds fluttered across his field of vision.
The old wolf could resist the call of the world no longer. Besides, he was hungry.
He crawled over to his mate and tried to persuade her to get up. But she only snarled at him, so he walked out into the bright sunshine alone.
He found the snow soft and the traveling difficult.
He spotted a rabbit, but his heavy body broke through the melting snow crust, and the rabbit scurried away.
When One Eye finally returned to the lair, it was nighttime, and he was hungrier than when he'd set out.
Strange sounds now came from inside the cave.
The sounds were not made by his mate, and yet they were somehow familiar. He stepped cautiously into the dark cave.
But he couldn't see much, and the she-wolf greeted him with a warning snarl.
Morning came and a dim light filled the cave. One Eye attempted once more to investigate the sounds.
Again his mate snarled a warning, and the old wolf kept a respectful distance.
Nevertheless, he was able to see, snuggled against the length of her body, five little bundles of life, very feeble, very helpless.
They were making tiny whimpering noises.
His mate eyed him anxiously. She growled softly, and when he approached too near, the growls shot up in her throat to a sharp snarl.
Though she did not know this, it was her instinct—an instinct passed down from many generations of wolf—to protect her young, even from their own father.
But there was no danger, because One Eye had his own instinct, which had been passed down to him from all the fathers of wolves.
He did not question it, nor puzzle over it. It was just there, a simple command to go out and find meat.
Several miles from the lair, the stream divided. Large fresh tracks led up the left fork.
One Eye knew that in the wake of such a trail there was little meat for him.
So he headed up the right fork, and his keen ears soon caught a gnawing sound.
He crept closer and found a porcupine eating bark.
As the wolf approached, the porcupine curled itself up, showing its sharp quills. One Eye knew this species of animal.
Once, in his youth, he'd sniffed too close and had a quill stuck in his muzzle for weeks; the pain had been fierce.
The wolf had never eaten a porcupine.
But there was such a thing as chance, so he lay down and waited silently, hoping for the moment when the porcupine might let its guard down.
But after half an hour, that moment hadn't come. So One Eye arose. He growled angrily at the motionless animal and trotted on.
In the afternoon he stumbled upon a bird, a ptarmigan. The startled bird tried to rise, but the wolf pounced quickly and caught it in his teeth.
He started to eat the bird, but then he remembered the small bundles of life in the lair. Carrying the bird in his mouth, he headed back downstream.
He came across more tracks—from the same animal he'd noticed earlier that day.
They went in the same direction he was going, so he moved silently, ever watchful.
As he came around some rocks, his eyes made out the maker of the tracks—a large female lynx.
She was crouched in front of the curled-up porcupine.
One Eye lay down in the snow, dropping the ptarmigan beside him, and watched, waiting to see if chance would provide him with an opportunity.
An hour passed, and still the porcupine, the lynx, and the wolf stayed frozen in place.
Despite their stillness all three animals were more alive than ever, each in its own fight for survival.
Then One Eye saw movement. Slowly, cautiously, the porcupine was uncurling itself!
In a flash the lynx slashed the porcupine's underside with its claws.
At that same moment, a flick of the porcupine's tail sank sharp quills into the lynx's paw.
One Eye started to rise as both animals squealed in pain. The lynx sprang savagely at the thing that had hurt her.
But the porcupine flicked its tail again, leaving the lynx's nose bristling with quills.
The big cat backed away, sneezing and pawing at her nose. She leaped about in pain and fright, desperately trying to knock out the quills.
Finally she sprang away, squalling with every leap she made.
When the lynx's cries faded in the distance, One Eye stalked toward the wounded porcupine.
The animal had curled itself up again, but its wound was deep, and it would not live long.
The wolf lay down and waited until the quills drooped and the porcupine's body relaxed.
Carefully he gripped the dead animal with his teeth and headed downstream.
Then he remembered the ptarmigan. He hurried back to where it lay, and ate it. He returned to the porcupine and carried it to the lair.
When the she-wolf saw the porcupine, she inspected it, turned her muzzle to the old wolf, and lightly licked him on the neck.
She trusted him now. He was behaving as a wolf-father should.
Right from the start, the gray cub was different from his brothers and sisters.
While their fur had a reddish hue inherited from the she-wolf, the gray cub looked like their father, like a true wolf.
When he was born, the gray cub's eyes weren't open, and yet he could feel, taste, and smell.
He knew his two brothers and two sisters very well. And he knew his mother—the source of all his nourishment.
She possessed a gentle, caressing tongue that soothed him as it passed over his soft little body.
Along with his siblings, he slept for most of his first month of life.
When their eyes opened, the cubs began to stay awake for longer periods of time.
The gray cub romped awkwardly with his brothers and sisters, making little growls.
His sight became clearer, and he realized that his world had another dweller, an old one-eyed wolf who often came and went.
The gray cub soon discovered that one wall of his dark little world was different from the other three.
This was the mouth of the cave and the source of light. Just as a plant grows toward the sun, the gray cub also felt compelled to move toward it.
Along with his siblings, he made a habit of crawling toward the mouth of the cave. But their mother never let them reach it.
It was in this way that the gray cub learned other things about his mother besides her soft, soothing tongue.
In his repeated attempts to crawl toward the light, he discovered a paw that could crush him down and roll him over with a swift stroke.
This was how he learned about hurt too, and how to avoid it.
He was a fierce little cub, and so were his brothers and sisters.
Like all wolves, they were carnivorous animals—meat-killers and meat-eaters.
But the gray cub was the fiercest of the litter.
He could growl louder than any of his brothers or sisters, and his tiny rages were much more terrible than theirs.
He was the first to learn the trick of rolling a fellow cub over with a cunning paw stroke.
And he was the first to grip another cub by the ear, pulling and tugging and growling through tightly clenched jaws.
Not surprisingly, he became the one who caused their mother the most trouble in keeping her litter away from the mouth of the cave.
Each day the gray cub became more and more fascinated by the light. And as quickly as he moved toward it, his mother drove him back.
The gray cub had no idea that the strange wall of light was an entrance.
He didn't know anything about entrances—passages that lead from one place to another place—because he did not know there was such a thing as another place.
And yet, like his mother and father, the gray cub was governed by instinct, and deep down inside, he knew he was destined to reach that wall.
There was one strange thing about the wall of light. The gray cub's father, the old one-eyed wolf, was able to walk through it and disappear.
The gray cub could not understand this. Even though his mother never let him approach the wall of light, she let him approach the other walls.
And any time he did so, his nose struck a hard surface. This hurt, and after several such adventures, the gray cub left the other walls alone.
Like most creatures of the wild, the gray cub experienced famine. A time came when there was little meat, and his mother stopped making milk.
At first the cubs whimpered and cried, but for the most part they slept.
There was no more playing, or tiny rages, or attempts at growling. The adventures toward the wall of light ceased.
The cubs slept, while the life that was in them began to fade.
As the effects of starvation worked on the gray cub and his siblings, One Eye ranged far and wide, desperate to find food to save his family.
He journeyed back to the Indian camp several times to steal rabbits from the snares.
But as the snow melted, and the streams began to flow, the people there packed up and moved away.
During this time the old wolf rarely slept in the lair, which by now had become cheerless and miserable.
The she-wolf too left her litter and went out in search of meat.
Eventually One Eye and the she-wolf began to return to the lair with small amounts of meat, and the gray cub soon regained his health.
When the cub was finally able to move around again, he found that the population of his world had grown smaller.
Three of his siblings were gone. Only he and one of his sisters had survived the famine.
The gray cub grew stronger but found himself forced to play alone, for his sister no longer lifted her head or moved about.
His little body rounded out with the meat he was now eating, but that food had come too late for her.
She slept continuously, growing weaker, until the life in her flickered lower and lower and finally died out.
Then there came a time when the gray cub no longer saw his father appearing and disappearing through the wall of light, nor sleeping in the entrance.
The she-wolf knew why One Eye never came back, but she had no way to explain this to her cub.
She'd been hunting for meat up the left fork of the stream, which was where the female lynx lived.
There the she-wolf had found her mate's footprints mixed with those of the lynx, and then, his remains.
The she-wolf had discovered something else along the left fork: the big cat's tracks led back up to a lair.
From outside the lair the she-wolf sniffed a litter of kittens. But she knew better than to enter.
Bad-tempered and vicious, a mother lynx would protect her young fiercely.
Still the wild is the wild, and motherhood is motherhood.
The she-wolf could fight just as fiercely as the lynx for the survival of her own young.
And a time would come when she'd have little choice but to enter that lair and face the lynx.
By the time his mother began leaving the cave to hunt, the cub knew to stay away from the entrance.
In his young mind, it was a law that must be obeyed. At first his mother had taught him this law. And then fear taught him.
This was a fear of the unknown, an instinct, passed down through thousands of generations of wolves.
As the cub lay alone in the cave, he'd occasionally hear some unseen animal sniffing from behind the wall of light.
The cub's eyes stayed trained on the entrance, and his hair bristled. But he always remained absolutely silent and still.
This was another instinct he had, one about knowing how to conceal himself.
As the cub grew, other forces were working on him.
His instinct and fear had taught him to obey the laws he'd learned, but soon his growth began to demand something new—disobedience.
So one day the cub stepped toward the wall of light.
Unlike other walls, the wall of light seemed to recede from the cub as he approached, and his nose didn't strike any hard surface.
The light grew brighter and then the wall was gone.
The cub stood in the entrance of the cave, gazing at a scene completely unfamiliar to him—dense forest, a mountain, the sky.
The cub felt dizzy. Everything was wide open, painfully bright, and much bigger.
The frightened cub crouched low and snarled at the wide new world in front of him.
But nothing happened. And soon the cub's eyes adjusted to the light, and he forgot to be scared.
As he continued to gaze out, he noticed a pine tree and the stream running by the cave. Curious, the cub took a step forward.
But the ground wasn't smooth like the ground in the lair, and the cub tumbled down a hill, yipping in pain.
When he got up, he investigated the grass under his feet, a berry bush, and a dead tree trunk.
The cub jumped back as a squirrel darted past him. The squirrel was just as scared, and scampered up a tree, chattering angrily at the cub.
The cub snarled at the small animal and moved on. He came across a gray bird and reached out his paw.
The bird pecked him on the nose, and the cub yipped in pain again.
As the bird flew away, the cub was left with new information. Some things were alive and some things were not.
He must be careful around the live things, because they could move, and he didn't know what they might do.
The cub traveled clumsily at first. He tripped on sticks.
Branches hit him on the nose and raked his side. Pebbles and stones shot upward as he stepped on them.
But with every trip and stumble, he was learning. Soon he walked with skill and confidence.
When he came across a nest of ptarmigan chicks, the cub felt a sensation of hunger.
The small ptarmigans made noises, scaring him at first. But he was a meat-eater, and his instinct was to hunt and to kill. He ate one of the birds.
The taste of it was good, so he ate another, and another, until he'd devoured every bird in the nest.
Happy from his meal, the cub licked his chops and headed away from the nest.
A flurry of feathers rushed at him. It was the mother ptarmigan, beating him with her wings! The cub hid his head between his paws and yelped.
But the furious bird continued her attack. Then the cub got angry too. He rose up snarling, and sank his teeth into one of the bird's wings.
The bird struggled, showering the cub with blows from its free wing. This was the small wolf's first battle, and he was elated.
He was doing exactly what he'd been born to do.
Then the ptarmigan pecked hard on the cub's nose. With a startled cry, he released the bird and ran away.
He turned back to look at the ptarmigan and felt a sudden rush of wind. A huge winged creature swooped down, barely missing the cub.
The hawk struck downward, and then darted up again, clutching the wounded ptarmigan in its talons.
The cub stayed hidden in a bush for a long time, frightened by the hawk's sudden attack. He had learned another lesson.
Small living things were meat, and they were good to eat. But big living things could cause pain, or even kill him. It was best to leave them alone.
The cub continued to explore and came to the stream, which appeared to be smooth.
He stepped onto it, only to feel it give way under his feet. He splashed into its icy depths and the current swept him downstream.
The water tossed him under and smashed him into rocks.
The cub thrashed, trying desperately to breathe, until the stream slowed and he reached a bank. He crawled clear of the water and lay down.
He had learned something else about the world. Water was not alive, but it moved. So things were not always what they appeared to be.
As the cub lay there, soaked and injured, he remembered his mother, the she-wolf.
And then there came to him a feeling that he wanted her more than anything else in the world.
Not only was his body tired from his adventures, but his young brain was tired too. Lonely and helpless, the little cub searched for his cave.
He was walking between some bushes when a flash of yellow appeared in front of him.
It was a weasel, a vicious and fast-moving animal. Before the cub could react, he felt the weasel's teeth in his neck.
The cub growled and shook his head furiously, but the small animal would not relax its grip.
Its teeth sank deeper and deeper, and the cub felt his body grow weak. His snarls faded into whimpers.
Swiftly and silently, the she-wolf bounded into view. Upon seeing her, the weasel let go of the cub and attempted to sprint away.
The she-wolf pounced and killed the small beast that had harmed her cub.
To the cub it seemed that his mother's joy at finding him was even greater than his own joy at being found.
She nuzzled him and caressed him and licked his wounds. Then mother and cub ate the weasel and returned home.
The cub was soon ranging far from the cave.
When he ran across the squirrel that had chattered at him on his first day out, the cub growled and snapped.
And whenever he spotted a gray bird, he remembered the peck he'd received on his nose, and flew into a wild rage.
Still, the young cub was usually cautious. The hawk's moving shadow always sent him crouching into the nearest thicket.
The cub now moved easily through the wilderness, his movements effortless and swift.
With hunting, however, he had run out of luck.
The ptarmigan chicks from his first adventure were the only prey he'd caught so far, and his desire to hunt grew each day.
He wanted very much to catch the squirrel.
The small animal's chatter always warned the other creatures when the cub approached.
The cub had the greatest respect for his mother. She could get meat, and she never failed to bring the cub his share.
And she wasn't afraid of anything. She had knowledge and strength, which to the cub, represented power.
She demanded obedience from him, and as he grew bigger, her temper grew shorter.
When the cub needed to be disciplined, she no longer used her paw; she used her fangs.
Famine came again, and once more the cub felt the pain of hunger. The she-wolf was gone for long periods of time, hoping to find meat.
At first the cub had hunted for play, for the sheer joy of it; now he hunted in deadly earnestness, and found nothing.
Yet this fierce hunger taught him many important things about hunting.
It made him study the habits of the squirrel closely, and he tried repeatedly to sneak up on it.
He studied mice and tried to dig them out of their burrows, and he studied birds.
His confidence grew until a day came when the hawk's shadow no longer scared him. He had grown stronger and wiser.
Also he was desperate. He knew that the hawk was meat, the meat his stomach needed.
So he sat on his haunches in a clearing, and challenged the hawk to come down from the sky.
But the hawk refused to come down and fight, and the cub whimpered with disappointment and hunger.
At last the famine broke, and the she-wolf brought home meat. This meat was different from any she had ever brought before.
It was a lynx kitten, a little smaller than the cub, and it was all for him. His mother had eaten all the other kittens in the litter.
The cub didn't know how desperate that action had been.
He knew only that the lynx was meat, and he ate happily. Then, with a full stomach, the cub snuggled close to his mother and slept.
He was aroused by a snarl from the she-wolf—the most vicious snarl he'd ever heard from her.
The cub looked up and saw the object of her anger and fear. In the full glare of the afternoon light, the lynx mother crouched in the cave's entrance.
The hair bristled along the cub's back as his mother stood facing the intruder. The lynx let out a low snarl that quickly rose to a raging screech.
Feeling suddenly brave, the young cub jumped to his feet and snarled valiantly by his mother's side. But she thrust him behind her.
The lynx rushed in, crawling low. The she-wolf sprang upon the large cat and pinned her down.
From the darkness at the rear of the cave, the cub saw little of the battle.
There was a tremendous snarling and spitting and screeching as the two animals thrashed about.
The she-wolf bit furiously with her sharp fangs while the lynx attacked not just with fangs, but with four sets of sharp claws.
The cub sprang in and sank his teeth into one of the lynx's hind legs. He clung on, growling savagely.
The two larger animals tumbled over, crushing the cub under their weight and knocking loose his hold.
The next moment the two mothers separated, and the lynx slashed the cub's shoulder with a huge forepaw.
Yelping in pain, the cub tumbled sidewise against the wall. Now frightened, he cowered in a corner as his mother continued to battle.
It wasn't long before the cub felt his courage return. Again he jumped in, biting deep into the lynx's hind leg.
The young wolf was growling furiously between his clenched teeth when he realized the lynx had stopped moving. The fierce creature was dead.
The she-wolf was weak and badly wounded.
At first she caressed the cub and licked his wounded shoulder, but the blood she'd lost in the fight had taken her strength.
She fell into a deep sleep. For two days she lay next to the dead lynx, without moving and barely breathing.
During the next week, she only left the cave for water. Her movements were slow and painful.
By the end of this time the lynx had been eaten, and the she-wolf's wounds had healed enough for her to venture out again to hunt.
The cub's shoulder was stiff and sore from the lynx's slash, and for a while he walked with a limp. But the world now seemed changed.
He went about with greater confidence, with a feeling of power and pride that he didn't have before the battle with the lynx.
He had buried his teeth in the flesh of an enemy, and he had survived. Along with his skills as a hunter, his skills as a fighter were growing.
The cub now accompanied his mother on hunting trips, and he soon realized there were two kinds of life—his own kind and the other kind.
His own kind included his mother and himself. The other kind included all living things that moved.
All living things that moved were meat, and from this the cub learned the essential law of meat: Eat or be eaten.
The hunt for meat, the fighting with other live things—these provided the cub with a great happiness.
It was the same happiness that having a full stomach or dozing in the sunshine provided.
The cub lived in a hostile environment, but he wasn't bothered by it.
Instead he felt very much alive, very happy, and very proud of himself.
The cub left the cave and ran down to the stream. Still half-asleep, he headed for the water automatically, without thinking much about the trail.
So by the time his nose caught the unfamiliar scent, it was too late.
Sitting in front of him were five live things, a species he'd never seen before—mankind.
The cub's first instinct was to run. But a second instinct sensed great power in these creatures and filled him with awe, a sense of his own smallness.
This instinct had been passed down from the wolves who, many generations ago, first wandered into a camp in order to sit by a warm fire. The cub did not move.
The men didn't seem to be afraid of the cub. One of the Indians approached him.
The cub instantly cowered, his lips curled, and sunlight sparkled on his little fangs.
The man laughed. "Look at the white fangs!"
The other men laughed too.
"Pick him up, Gray Beaver," one man said.
As the man named Gray Beaver reached out, the cub snapped, biting the man's hand.
Immediately the cub felt a sharp blow to the side of his head. Frightened, the cub cried out for his mother.
The man hit him again, and the cub cried louder. Then he heard the she-wolf approaching fast.
The cub stopped his crying, waiting for the arrival of his mother—his fierce protector who fought and killed all things and was never afraid.
When the she-wolf bounded into view, the men moved backward, clearly scared. The cub uttered a glad little cry and ran to meet her.
The she-wolf faced the men, her hair bristling and a snarl rumbling deep in her throat.
Gray Beaver's eyes opened wide in surprise. He cried out, "Kiche!"
Then his look grew stern, and again he said, "Kiche!" But this time he spoke with authority and sharpness.
The cub watched in horror as his mother crouched down, whimpering and wagging her tail.
Gray Beaver stepped forward and put his hand on her head. The she-wolf didn't growl or snap. The cub could not understand this.
The other men moved closer.
"It's been a year since she ran away," one man said.
Gray Beaver nodded. "There was a famine, and we had no meat for the dogs. She ran off to take care of herself. It's not surprising. She's half-wolf."
"And she's been living with wolves," a third man said, pointing at the wolf cub.
Gray Beaver nodded. "This cub's father must be a wolf, so there is little dog in him. His fangs are white. He will be called White Fang."
The man put his hand on the cub's head, and out of fear of another beating, the cub allowed it.
As the big hand rubbed behind his ears, the cub almost enjoyed the sensation.
"Kiche was my brother's dog," Gray Beaver said. "And now my brother is dead. So Kiche and this cub are mine. I have spoken."
Gray Beaver tied Kiche to a stick, and then the group made their way through the woods until they met up with other people.
A group of dogs immediately rushed at White Fang, slashing and biting him with their fangs.
The cub cried out for help. He heard his mother growl, and then the sounds of the men yelling.
Using stones and heavy clubs, the men drove away the attacking dogs.
Until this time the cub had thought his mother, his siblings, and One Eye were the only others of his kind.
But now there were more, and they'd attacked him!
Yet the men had saved him. So the cub decided that these men had the power to make and enforce laws.
Unlike other animals, they didn't use fangs or claws. They had the power to make dead things—sticks and stones—do their bidding.
The group headed downstream until they arrived at a clearing. Kiche was tied to a stick in the ground, and the cub sat by her.
He watched with fear and awe as the people raised poles and wrapped them in cloth and skins.
Soon massive tepees filled the cub's field of vision.
At first these enormous objects scared the young wolf. But then his fear subsided, and he left his mother's side to explore.
White Fang saw other dogs try to enter tepees, only to be chased away by the women inside.
The cub grabbed the side of one tepee with his teeth and pulled hard.
It shook, which gave the cub a thrill until he heard an angry voice shout from inside. After that he left the tepees alone.
White Fang encountered another puppy, a bit larger than himself.
The puppy didn't seem dangerous, so White Fang approached him in a friendly way.
But then the puppy bared his fangs, and White Fang did the same.
The two circled each other, snarling until the puppy leaped in, slashed the cub, and leaped back away.
White Fang charged at the puppy, snapping viciously. But the puppy had fought many fights.
He bit White Fang repeatedly until the cub ran back to his mother. The cub would later hear the men call the puppy Lip-lip.
After recovering from his fight, White Fang left his mother's side to explore some more.
He found Gray Beaver squatting over a pile of sticks. Other people sat nearby. The cub approached cautiously.
A strange mist rose from the sticks beneath Gray Beaver's hands. Then a thing that appeared to be alive flickered into view.
Bright as the sun, it danced and twisted before White Fang's eyes.
This was fire, and curiosity about it drew the cub closer. After poking his nose into the flames, the cub fell backward, crying in pain.
Gray Beaver laughed loudly and slapped his thighs, and soon others laughed too. White Fang felt ashamed.
He knew he was being laughed at, and the pain of that was worse than the burn he'd received.
He fled to Kiche, the one creature in the camp who was not laughing at him.
That night White Fang lay by his mother's side, feeling homesick.
The camp had a continuous buzz of movement, and he missed the quiet and stillness of the wilderness.
And the people—they were not like other animals. They built tepees and changed the surface of the land.
From dead sticks, Gray Beaver had also made a moving, burning thing—fire—appear. These people held power over dogs and demanded obedience.
They were not ordinary animals; these fire-makers were gods.
The days went by, and White Fang learned more about the ways of people. When they walked, he got out of their way.
When they called, he came. And when they threatened, he cowered.
He knew these godly and superior creatures had the power to enforce—with club or stone—any command they made.
He was getting used to his new life, but the wild still called to him. He often crept to the edge of the forest and listened, wishing to be out there.
But he always returned to camp, restless and confused, and lay by his mother. She was still tied up.
The worst part of the cub's life was the puppy Lip-lip.
Whenever White Fang ventured away from his mother, Lip-lip was waiting for him, ready to bully and torment him.
The puppy was bigger than White Fang, so even though the wolf cub always fought back, he never won any of these battles.
The other young dogs in camp let out their energy by running and playing with one another.
This activity, however, was denied to White Fang. Any time the cub tried to play with the others, Lip-lip drove him away with growls and fangs.
As a result, White Fang became withdrawn and antisocial, and his life in the camp was miserable.
Older dogs often took his food, so he became crafty, sneaking around the camp and stealing from people when they weren't looking.
A day came when Gray Beaver decided to untie White Fang's mother.
"I do not believe you will run away, Kiche," he said.
Once again Kiche could roam freely with White Fang. That afternoon they went to the edge of the woods.
The cub ran a short distance among the trees, stopped, and looked back. He called to his mother, begging her to follow. She didn't move.
He whined and scurried playfully in and out of the underbrush. He ran back to her, licked her face, and went back into the trees.
But still she wouldn't follow. He stopped and regarded her eagerly, but that eagerness faded when she turned her head and trotted back toward camp.
White Fang sat down in the shadow of a birch tree, and whimpered softly. He was still only a cub, and he needed his mother.
At last he got up and followed her back into the camp, pausing now and again to listen to the sounds of the forest.
In the wild a wolf cub only stays with its mother for a short time. When living with people, the cub's time with its mother can be even shorter.
Gray Beaver was in debt to a man named Three Eagles.
Three Eagles was leaving the camp, so Gray Beaver gave him a bearskin, some ammunition—and Kiche.
When White Fang saw his mother taken aboard Three Eagles' canoe, he tried to follow her.
A blow from Three Eagles knocked him backward. The canoe departed.
Horrified of losing his mother, White Fang plunged into the water and swam after the canoe.
Gray Beaver shouted angrily, "White Fang! Get back here!"
But the young cub ignored him. Gray Beaver launched a canoe and quickly caught up to White Fang.
He grabbed the cub by the nape of the neck and beat him. Finally Gray Beaver flung the cub into the canoe and started to paddle back to camp.
When the man's foot bumped into White Fang, the cub bit it.
White Fang knew immediately that he'd made a terrible mistake. Gray Beaver beat him more savagely this time.
The cub cried in pain and fright under the angry blows, and then he fell silent.
Back on land, White Fang was bruised and limping. Right away, Lip-lip lunged, knocking him over and sinking sharp fangs into him.
White Fang was too helpless to defend himself, and would have died if Gray Beaver hadn't intervened.
The man kicked Lip-lip hard, sending him hurtling more than a dozen feet away. In his pitiful state, White Fang felt a sense of gratitude.
He'd also learned another law: never bite the flesh of his gods.
White Fang again tried to settle into his new life with these gods.
They demanded strict obedience, and as long as White Fang submitted to that one law, he would avoid pain.
He still missed his old life in the wild, and he missed Kiche terribly.
Every now and then he wandered into the forest to cry out and mourn the loss of her.
He'd seen people leave the camp and then come back, so he held onto the hope that one day she too might return.
Day after day, with Lip-lip leading the charge, the dogs attacked White Fang.
The cub knew that if he lost his footing, he'd lose his life, so he became an expert at keeping his feet beneath him at all times.
White Fang's feet skidded across the dirt as the dogs threw the weight of their bodies into him.
But they never succeeded in knocking him over.
His fighting skills improved, and he fought viciously. When he attacked, he did so without warning, leaping in, slashing, and leaping back out.
The dogs grew to fear White Fang, but when they were in a large group, they chased him.
If one unlucky dog accidentally ran ahead of the pack, White Fang spun around and attacked.
Then he'd start running again before the rest of the dogs caught up.
He often led these chases into the forest, where his knowledge of the wild helped him to outsmart the camp dogs.
Gliding silently among the twisted shrubs and fallen trees, he'd quickly throw the camp dogs off his trail.
Then he'd lie in a thicket, surrounded by their confused cries.
Any lone dog who wandered too close to White Fang found itself bitten and slashed, or worse—dead.
When the wolf cub killed his first victim, there was a great commotion in the camp. Some men were furious and demanded vengeance.
But Gray Beaver hid the cub in his tepee and wouldn't let anyone get near him.
White Fang was an outcast, hated by nearly everyone—dog and human.
Almost no kindness or affection was ever shown to him, and none was allowed to grow in him.
He stalked about snarling, with his ears flattened and his lips curled up, always ready for an attack.
He became quicker, craftier, and deadlier than the other dogs. He was lean, with muscles like iron, and he was cruel.
He had to be this way—it was the only way he could survive in such a harsh environment.
Summer came to an end and fall set in. The days grew shorter, the nights longer, and the bite of frost filled the air.
The camp buzzed with activity. Tepees came down, and bags were packed into canoes.
White Fang didn't know it, of course, but the people were dismantling their summer camp in order to travel downstream for fall hunting.
As the first canoes disappeared down the river, White Fang saw his chance for freedom.
When nobody was looking, the cub slipped out of camp and into the woods. He came to a stream, and by walking through it, he hid his trail.
Then he crawled into a dense thicket and waited.
Hours passed and White Fang drifted off to sleep. He was awakened by voices.
"White Fang!" Gray Beaver called.
The cub remained silent.
Gray Beaver's son, Mit-sah, yelled too. "White Fang! Where are you?"
The shouts continued, and White Fang trembled with fear. He was disobeying his gods!
There was an impulse to crawl out of hiding and return to his master, but he resisted it.
Eventually the voices died away, and after waiting a while, the cub crawled out of his hiding spot.
Darkness was coming on, and for a while, he ran playfully among the trees, taking great pleasure in his freedom.
Then, suddenly, White Fang felt lonely and cold. Dark shadows hung over the silent forest, and danger seemed to lurk behind every tree.
In his mind he saw the camp again. The tepees stood tall, and the fires blazed with warmth. Voices spoke and laughed.
Dogs snarled and bickered. The cub felt hungry, and he remembered the pieces of meat and fish that people had thrown to him.
Now there was no meat—just a threatening silence.
He jumped with fright as a large dark mass moved through the forest.
It was the shadow of a tree, caused by the moon, which had just come out from behind the clouds.
The cub whimpered softly. Then, afraid that his whimpering might attract a new danger, he fell silent.
Crack! A branch fell from a tree and crashed near White Fang. He yelped in fright.
A panic seized him, and he ran madly back toward the village.
He felt a strong desire for the protection and companionship of the people.
In his nostrils was the smell of smoke; in his ears, were the voices of people. He bounded out of the forest and into the moonlit clearing.
But no camp greeted his eyes. He had forgotten—the people had gone away.
White Fang stopped running. He slunk sadly through the deserted camp, smelling the rubbish heaps and discarded items of his gods.
He would have been glad to have a stone thrown at him by an angry woman, glad for a beating from Gray Beaver.
He would have even welcomed the sight of Lip-lip and the whole snarling pack.
He came to where Gray Beaver's tepee had stood, and sat down. White Fang pointed his nose at the moon.
His mouth opened and out came a heartbroken cry, filled with fear, loneliness, and grief for his lost mother. It was White Fang's first howl.
Daylight came, and the bare earth where the camp had stood looked more desolate in the morning light. White Fang knew what he must do.
He plunged into the forest and followed the riverbank downstream, hoping to catch the trail of his gods. All day he ran without any rest.
His lean body ignored fatigue, for he was a wolf, blessed with the gift of endurance.
Just as his mother and father had run for days in search of meat, White Fang ran now in search of his gods.
The riverbank gave way to steep cliffs. White Fang climbed over mountains until a path led him back to the river.
A thin sheet of ice was beginning to form, allowing him to travel on the river in some areas.
More than once, though, he crashed through and struggled for life in the icy current.
He journeyed farther and farther, always on the lookout for the trail of his people.
He knew that somewhere along the river, they would land their canoes and head inland.
The sun went down, and White Fang ran through another night, bounding through shrubs and over fallen trees.
By the middle of the second day he had been running continuously for thirty hours, and his body was beginning to give out.
The broad pads of his feet were bruised and bleeding, causing him to run with a limp.
It had been forty hours since his last meal, and he was weak with hunger. His coat was wet and dirty from his repeated falls into the icy water.
The sky turned gray, and snow began to fall, obscuring the details of the terrain.
White Fang slipped and stumbled, and traveling became more painful.
Night fell again, and the snow came down more thickly. White Fang whimpered softly as he limped along.
Finally he spotted a fresh set of tracks in the snow, leading inland, away from the river.
He recognized them right away. Whining with eagerness, he followed the tracks into the forest.
The sounds of a camp came to his ears. He saw the blaze of a fire, and Gray Beaver's wife, Kloo-kooch, cooking.
Gray Beaver was squatting in front of the fire and eating.
White Fang expected a beating. He crouched and bristled at the thought of it. Then he went forward again.
He feared being beaten, but it would be worth it.
Once again he'd have the comfort of a fire, food to eat, and the protection of his gods.
Gray Beaver saw him and stopped eating. White Fang lay at his master's feet, trembling.
Gray Beaver moved his hand. The cub cringed, expecting a blow.
It did not fall. He glanced up. Gray Beaver was tearing off a piece of meat!
The man offered it to White Fang. Gently, and somewhat suspiciously, the cub sniffed the meat, and then proceeded to eat it.
As the cub ate heartily, his god stood over him, guarding him from the other dogs who would have otherwise stolen the meat.
Then, feeling grateful and content, White Fang lay at Gray Beaver's feet and gazed at the warm fire.
The cub knew that tomorrow he would not be alone in the bleak wilderness.
He would be in the camp of the people, the gods upon whom White Fang was now completely dependent.
That winter Gray Beaver and his family headed out on a journey to some other villages.
Gray Beaver drove one sled, pulled by a team of older dogs, while his son, Mit-sah, drove a smaller one.
Mit-sah's sled was pulled by seven puppies—including White Fang and Lip-lip.
White Fang didn't mind the work. He had run himself nearly to death to be reunited with his gods, and he knew it was pointless to disobey them.
By now he'd forgotten about Kiche and living in the wild. His allegiance was to his gods, so he worked hard and obeyed their laws.
Mit-sah made Lip-lip the leader of his team. This might have seemed an honor, but it was really a punishment.
The boy had watched Lip-lip torment White Fang many times in the past, and now he was avenging the treatment of the wolf cub.
As the leader, Lip-lip had to run ahead of the other puppies.
Now, instead of seeing Lip-lip's bristling mane and sharp fangs, the puppies saw his bushy tail and fleeing hind legs.
To their eyes, he appeared to be running from them, which triggered an instinct to chase.
The faster Lip-lip ran, the faster the others ran, growling and snapping at his legs.
When Lip-lip turned to snarl at them, Mit-sah sent out a stinging lash with his whip.
Lip-lip had no choice but to run fast and stay ahead of the team.
Each night Mit-sah gave Lip-lip extra meat, not to reward him but to make the rest of the team hate him even more.
It worked, and each morning the puppies chased Lip-lip with a renewed fury.
White Fang could have stepped in and become the leader of the pack.
But he was too solitary and ill-tempered for that. He either attacked his teammates, or ignored them.
They got out of his way when he came along, and none of them ever dared to steal his meat.
On the contrary, they devoured their own meat quickly for fear that he would take it away from them.
White Fang lived by a law: to oppress the weak and obey the strong. Among the puppies he was a ruthless tyrant.
But when older, bigger dogs were around, he knew to walk softly and show respect.
Months passed, and the team visited many villages. White Fang grew strong from the long hours pulling the sled, and his mind grew sharp.
He had no affection for Gray Beaver. The man was a god, but he was a savage god.
He did not speak kind words or caress with gentle hands.
When White Fang thought of hands, he thought of pain. It was true that the hands sometimes gave meat, but more often they gave hurt.
Hands were things to keep away from. They hurled stones, held clubs and whips, delivered slaps and blows.
But White Fang remembered the law: never bite the flesh of his gods. Doing so was an unforgivable crime.
During a stay in one village, however, White Fang learned to modify this law.
Shortly after the team arrived in a village, all the dogs were free to wander and forage for food.
White Fang came across a boy who was chopping frozen moose meat with an axe.
Chips of frozen meat landed in the snow, and White Fang stopped to eat them.
Then he saw the boy lay down the axe and pick up a club. White Fang sprang away, just in time to escape the boy's blow.
The boy chased White Fang, and the cub ran until he found himself trapped between two tepees. Ready to strike, the boy moved toward the wolf.
White Fang was furious. He faced the boy, bristling and snarling.
He knew the law of forage: all wasted meat, such as the frozen chips, belonged to the dog who found it.
White Fang had done nothing wrong, broken no law, yet this boy was about to give him a beating.
White Fang hardly knew what happened next. He did it with a burst of rage.
And he did it so quickly that the boy was uncertain how it happened too.
In an instant the boy was lying in the snow, his hand ripped wide open by White Fang's teeth.
The boy cried out in pain. White Fang realized that he'd just broken the law of the gods—he had bitten the flesh of a god!
White Fang ran back to Gray Beaver's camp, expecting a terrible punishment.
When the bitten boy arrived with his family, White Fang cowered behind Gray Beaver's legs.
He listened as the two families shouted at each other. Then he understood that Gray Beaver was defending him.
That's when the cub realized there was a difference between his gods and other gods.
White Fang had to obey his own gods. But he did not have to allow other gods to treat him unfairly.
Later that day Mit-sah was alone, gathering firewood in the forest, when the boy who'd been bitten arrived with some friends.
After another argument the boys attacked Mit-sah.
At first White Fang watched, not sure what to do. This was a fight between the gods; it didn't concern him.
But then he realized that this was Mit-sah, one of his own gods, who was being attacked.
A mad rush of anger sent White Fang leaping in among the attackers.
Within moments the boys ran away, many of them dripping blood in the snow.
When Mit-sah told the story in camp, Gray Beaver ordered meat to be given to White Fang.
As White Fang lay by the fire, sleepy and with a full belly, he knew that he'd done something good. He had defended one of his gods against other gods.
From then on, he took his role of protector seriously. He protected not just Gray Beaver and his family, but their property as well.
If he saw another god preparing to steal from Gray Beaver, White Fang attacked with fury.
Months went by, and the bond between White Fang and Gray Beaver became stronger and stronger.
The terms of their agreement were simple: Gray Beaver offered food and fire, protection and companionship.
In return, White Fang obeyed Gray Beaver, protected him and his family, and guarded their possessions.
White Fang did not love Gray Beaver; he simply served him.
Spring arrived and Gray Beaver's family returned to the home camp. White Fang was now a year old and the largest dog on Mit-sah's sled team.
One day when an older dog tried to steal meat from White Fang, the young wolf attacked without thinking. The older dog snarled and his hair bristled.
White Fang, still feeling young and small, cowered as the large dog moved closer. But when the dog sniffed the meat, anger swelled in White Fang.
The wolf had ruled over his teammates for months. Now a dog was trying to steal from him!
White Fang knocked the dog to the ground, and bit deep.
When the dog finally broke free, he ran away whimpering, his tail tucked between his legs.
After that White Fang no longer cowered when walking among the older dogs. He stepped with confidence, unafraid of any of them.
The puppies had to stay out of the way of the older dogs, and tolerate having their meat stolen.
But not White Fang—in the eyes of the older dogs, he was now an equal.
In midsummer White Fang returned from a hunting trip to find a new tepee at the edge of the camp.
He trotted over to investigate and found himself face-to-face with Kiche.
He paused and looked at her. He remembered her vaguely, but she didn't seem to have any memory of him.
As her lip curled back, a rush of old memories flooded the young wolf's mind. This was his mother!
He bounded toward her joyously, but she met him with sharp fangs that slashed open his cheek. Puzzled, he backed away.
This was not Kiche's fault. A wolf-mother is not made to remember her cubs from previous years.
Kiche had a new litter of cubs, and her instinct now was to protect them.
One of the cubs clambered over to White Fang. White Fang sniffed the cub curiously, and Kiche attacked again. He backed farther away.
As Kiche licked her cub, White Fang's memories receded. The role Kiche had played in his life was forgotten. He had learned to get along without her.
Kiche attacked again, and White Fang backed away again.
He still remembered the law that forbade him from fighting with a female of his kind. Finally the young wolf turned his head and left.
The months went by, and Gray Beaver came to prize White Fang above all the other dogs.
The wolf was strong and ferocious. His one weakness, however, was that he could not stand being laughed at by the gods.
If White Fang heard men laughing at him, he would fly into a terrible rage.
He knew never to take out this anger on his gods, so it was the other dogs who suffered his wrath at these times.
When White Fang was three years old, there was a famine among the Indians. In the summer they found no fish in the river.
In the winter the caribou didn't follow their usual migration route, leaving the Indians with nothing to hunt. The situation in the camp was dire.
The women and children went hungry so that the men could eat and have strength for their search for meat.
Eventually the gods ate their leather moccasins and mittens, and the dogs ate the sled harnesses.
Any dog too weak to fight became prey, both for the gods and other dogs.
The wisest and strongest dogs abandoned the camp and fled into the wild. Many dogs were hunted and eaten by wolves.
In this time of misery, White Fang fled into the wilderness. He was better suited to this life than the other dogs, for he had been raised in the wild.
He excelled at stalking small living things. He'd lie concealed for hours, waiting for a squirrel to appear.
When he couldn't find squirrels, White Fang dug wood mice from their burrows. On more than one occasion, he returned to the camp.
But he did not go to sit near the fire.
Instead he lurked in the nearby forest, robbing any snare that held a hanging rabbit.
During his days in the wild, White Fang came across a half-starved wolf. The two animals considered each other for a moment.
Then White Fang ran the wolf down, killed him, and ate him.
Days later White Fang fought with a lynx and won.
For two days he feasted on this kill, which made him strong enough to outrun the hungry wolf pack that chased him down the following day.
During the chase White Fang managed to circle around and sneak up on one of his exhausted pursuers, killing and devouring him.
While every other creature in the wild seemed to suffer and fall prey to starvation, White Fang thrived.
White Fang wandered far, and eventually wound up in the valley where he'd been born.
He came across his old lair and found Kiche with one surviving cub. She too had fled to the wild.
She snarled at White Fang, and he moved on, eventually arriving at the lair of the lynx that he and Kiche had fought and killed so long ago.
Finding the lair empty, White Fang settled in to rest for a day.
Spring arrived and then came summer. One bright afternoon White Fang came around a large rock and saw Lip-lip.
No longer large and frightening, the wolf's enemy now looked weak and miserable.
Remembering all the suffering he'd endured from Lip-lip, White Fang felt his hair bristle. His lip curled, and a low snarl broke the silence.
As Lip-lip started to back away, White Fang struck, sinking his teeth deep into the dog's throat.
He then circled around his old enemy, watching the life flicker out of him.
A week later White Fang came to the edge of the forest, where a stretch of open land sloped down to the river.
There was a camp, and White Fang knew right away it was the camp of his gods, set up in a new location.
But the smells and sounds were different from those during the famine.
Now White Fang heard laughter. The smell of fish cooking filled the air.
White Fang hurried into the camp and looked for Gray Beaver's tepee. Gray Beaver wasn't there, but his wife, Kloo-Kooch, was.
"White Fang!" she cried out, glad to see him. "You've returned!"
She brought over a whole fish, and White Fang ate it heartily. Then he lay down and waited for his master to return.
If there had ever been a possibility of White Fang's getting along with the other dogs, it was destroyed when Mit-sah made him leader of the sled team.
Now the other dogs hated him, just as they'd grown to hate Lip-lip.
They hated the wolf for the extra meat he received from Mit-sah, and they hated him for always fleeing in front of them.
When the dogs saw White Fang's face—his curling lip and sharp fangs—they cowered in fear.
But the sight of his hindquarters had a different effect; it drove them to chase, hunt, and try to kill.
"Go!" Mit-sah cried each day.
The dogs lunged forward, pulling the sled and snapping viciously at the wolf.
When White Fang turned to fight back, Mit-sah's whip snapped in his face.
Running from the other dogs went against every instinct in the wolf. But he had no choice.
By the end of each day, White Fang's body was marred from being repeatedly bitten.
In camp at night, a typical sled team leader would huddle close to the gods, away from the other dogs.
But White Fang looked down on such protection.
He walked boldly among the other dogs, punishing them each night for what he had suffered during the day.
He hated the other dogs, and he hated being the leader of the team.
The dogs faced him as a pack for they knew he was too strong, too ferocious, for any one of them to fight alone.
But even in a large group, the dogs were no match for White Fang. The wolf was too quick for them, and too wise.
He avoided tight places and always knew to back away before he was surrounded. The constant battles molded White Fang into a vicious killer.
Gray Beaver marveled at the wolf, for the Indian himself was fierce and strong. "Never have I seen an animal as savage as White Fang," he declared.
When White Fang was nearly five years old, Gray Beaver took him on another long journey.
The trouble White Fang made among the dogs in the various villages was remembered for many years.
The wolf loved to terrorize other dogs.
The dogs who were not familiar with White Fang often bristled when he appeared, snarling and walking with stiff legs.
These are normal actions for a dog preparing to fight. But White Fang always skipped this stage.
As soon as an unsuspecting dog threatened or challenged him, the wolf instantly leaped in for the throat.
Because of White Fang's efficient speed and focus, none of the dogs stood a chance against him.
Gray Beaver traveled far that winter and spent the spring hunting in the mountains.
When the ice broke up and the rivers began to flow, he built a canoe and paddled downstream until he arrived at the Yukon River.
Along the bank was the village of Fort Yukon, an old trading post with a fort.
Gray Beaver had heard tales of a massive gold rush.
Thousands of men, from all over the world, were traveling up the Yukon River, headed for the Klondike territory, where they hoped to find gold and get rich.
Gray Beaver had piles of furs, mittens, and moccasins that he intended to trade.
Upon arriving in the village, he was thrilled to find that his goods were in high demand. Men were willing to pay much more than he'd hoped.
"I can make a big profit here," Gray Beaver murmured.
While Gray Beaver was busy trading, White Fang found himself with no work to do.
He wandered the streets of Fort Yukon, along with other Indian dogs.
At first White Fang was wary of this new place.
The village was much busier than the Indian camps he'd lived in. Instead of tepees, the village contained structures made from logs.
Crowds of men swarmed the muddy streets. The men looked and smelled different from Gray Beaver.
Their skin was lighter, and they wore different clothes.
At first the wolf kept his distance from these men, but after seeing other dogs approach them without being harmed, he relaxed.
As White Fang trotted along a street, men began to point at him.
"Look over there!"
"That dog looks just like a wolf!"
