Occasionally the white men approached White Fang, their hands outstretched.
White Fang backed away slowly, his teeth bared and a snarl rising from his throat.
None of the men succeeded in laying a hand on him, and it was fortunate that they did not.
It soon became clear to White Fang that very few of these gods—not more than a dozen—lived permanently at Fort Yukon.
The majority of them were traveling through on their way to the Klondike. Every couple of days, a steamship arrived with more passengers.
They'd spend several hours in the village before continuing up the river. To White Fang, there seemed to be an endless number of these men.
The dogs accompanying the men came in strange shapes and sizes. And none of them knew how to fight.
Whenever a steamship pulled in, White Fang and the rest of the Indian dogs hurried to the dock and waited for an unsuspecting dog to come down the gangway.
Upon seeing White Fang—a wolf—most new dogs started barking, and then rushed in for an attack.
White Fang sprang quickly to the new dog's side. For a brief moment, the attacking dog wondered what had become of the wolf.
It was in that moment that White Fang struck, rolling the dog off its feet and sinking his teeth into its throat.
The wolf then slinked away as the rest of the pack finished the dog off.
The men from the steamships grew angry when their dogs were killed.
They rushed into the dogfights, beating the Indian dogs with stones and clubs.
One man was so furious; he pulled out a revolver and fired six shots.
Afterward, six of White Fang's fellow dogs lay dead.
White Fang was never beaten for these attacks. Smarter than the other dogs in the pack, he knew to escape before the gods arrived.
To White Fang, this was all fun. He enjoyed killing the dogs that arrived on the steamships.
And he enjoyed watching from a safe distance as other Indian dogs got beaten and kicked for the crimes that White Fang had started.
The men who lived year-round in Fort Yukon disliked the newcomers who had come north, hoping to find gold and get rich.
But these residents did enjoy watching the havoc that the Indian dogs caused when the gold-seekers' dogs arrived.
One man enjoyed the dogfights more than anyone else. When the whistle of an approaching steamship blew, he was the first at the dock.
As dogs slashed and bit, yelping in pain, dying in the street, he cried out in delight.
No one knew this man's real name, so they called him Beauty Smith. But he was not beautiful at all.
He was short, with a small head. His large eyes were set far apart, and his crooked teeth were yellow and rotten.
His two upper canines were longer than the rest of his teeth, giving the impression of fangs.
His hair, which stuck out in patches, was the color of mud.
Beauty Smith did all the cooking and cleaning at the fort.
Even though he was weak and cowardly, the other men feared him.
Beauty was an angry man, and nobody would have been surprised if he did something terrible one day, like slip poison into the coffee.
Beauty paid particular attention to White Fang.
"With an animal that vicious," the man thought, "there's money to be made."
Beauty approached White Fang, reaching out and speaking softly.
The wolf bristled and bared his teeth. White Fang sensed something in this man—it was something evil.
White Fang was dozing in Gray Beaver's camp one day when he heard Beauty's footsteps approaching.
The wolf's hair bristled. As the man entered the camp, White Fang got up and moved to the edge of the forest.
He watched Beauty speaking with Gray Beaver. Beauty pointed at White Fang, and the wolf snarled.
Beauty laughed.
White Fang glided a short distance into the forest, keeping his eyes locked on Beauty.
"I will not sell White Fang," Gray Beaver said. "He's the strongest sled dog I've ever owned. And he can fight. There's no other dog like him."
"I'm willing to pay handsomely," Beauty cooed.
Gray Beaver folded his arms. "I have all the money I need. White Fang is not for sale, not for any price."
The following day Beauty returned with something that Gray Beaver did want—whiskey.
The whiskey seemed to take over the Indian's body. It wasn't long before he needed it, just as he needed air.
When one bottle was empty, Gray Beaver hurried into the village to buy another. His bag of money grew lighter and lighter until finally it was empty.
As Gray Beaver sat in his camp, alone and bankrupt, Beauty returned.
Again he asked to buy White Fang. But this time he offered to pay in whiskey, not money.
Gray Beaver nodded sadly. "If you can catch him, you can take him."
For the next few days, Beauty Smith followed White Fang. White Fang didn't know why.
He simply knew the man was evil. The wolf never let him come close.
Two days later Beauty brought more whiskey to Gray Beaver.
"You catch him," Beauty said.
White Fang slinked into camp one evening and was happy to see that Beauty was not there. The wolf lay down.
Suddenly he felt Gray Beaver tie a leather thong around his neck.
Gray Beaver sat down beside the wolf, holding the end of the thong in his hand. In the other hand he held a bottle, from which he occasionally drank.
An hour had passed when White Fang heard the familiar footsteps of Beauty approaching.
Gray Beaver's eyes were closed. But as the wolf tried to move away, Gray Beaver woke up and tightened his grip on the thong.
Beauty strode into camp and stood over White Fang. The wolf snarled.
One of the man's hands extended outward and began to descend upon White Fang's head. The snarl grew louder, angrier.
The hand continued down, while White Fang crouched beneath it. Suddenly White Fang snapped upward, striking the hand with his fangs.
The hand was jerked back, and White Fang's teeth came together with a sharp empty click.
Beauty was frightened and angry. Gray Beaver hit White Fang on the head, and the wolf cowered down in obedience.
White Fang watched Beauty go away and return with a stout club. Gray Beaver handed the end of the thong to the man. Beauty started to walk away.
He pulled on the thong, but White Fang refused to follow. Gray Beaver hit the wolf repeatedly.
Finally White Fang got up and rushed toward Beauty. Beauty swung the club and smashed White Fang down upon the ground.
Gray Beaver laughed and nodded his approval.
Beauty pulled the thong again, and this time White Fang followed meekly, his tail tucked between his legs.
The wolf continued to snarl, but he didn't attack. This god knew how to handle a club.
As they walked, Beauty kept a careful eye on White Fang.
The wolf kept an eye on the club. They arrived at the fort. Beauty tied up White Fang and then went to bed.
White Fang waited an hour. Then he chewed through the thong and trotted back to Gray Beaver's camp.
The wolf owed no allegiance to this new god—he belonged to Gray Beaver.
But again Gray Beaver tied a thong around White Fang's neck, and in the morning turned him over to Beauty.
This time Beauty gave the wolf a terrible beating. The evil god seemed to enjoy it. White Fang knew why he was being beaten.
He knew that it was Gray Beaver's will for him to go with this new god.
But the bond White Fang had with Gray Beaver was not easily broken.
Back at the fort, Beauty tied up White Fang again. Again the wolf broke free and returned to his master.
And again Gray Beaver placed the thong around his neck.
The beating White Fang received from Beauty the next morning was the worst he'd ever suffered.
For the entire time, Gray Beaver sat by, saying nothing, offering no protection. When the evil man was finished, the wolf could hardly walk.
Half-blind and limping, he followed his new god back to the fort.
He was secured with a heavy chain. Despite pulling and biting at the iron links, White Fang couldn't free himself.
After a few days, Gray Beaver's whiskey ran out. Miserable and with no money, he launched his canoe and paddled back upstream.
White Fang was now the property of a new god—a terrible, evil god.
Beauty Smith kept White Fang chained in a pen behind the fort. Day after day the evil god tormented the wolf.
"You miserable dog!" Beauty shouted as he swung his club.
When White Fang was worked into a rage, Beauty laughed. This made the wolf angrier still.
After noticing this, Beauty made it a point to laugh at the wolf at every opportunity.
More ferocious than ever, White Fang was in a constant state of fury. His hatred used to be reserved for other dogs.
Now the hatred extended to all things, both living and nonliving. He hated the chain that bound him. He hated the wooden slats of his pen.
And he hated the men who came to look at him. But most of all, above anything else, he hated Beauty Smith.
Beauty had a reason for this harsh treatment. White Fang did not know it, but the god was training him for something.
One day a group of men gathered outside the pen. Beauty entered, club in hand, and removed the chain from White Fang's neck.
After Beauty left the pen, White Fang tore around, growling and snapping, trying to get at the men outside.
The door of the pen opened again. White Fang paused. Something unexpected was happening. The door opened wider.
Then a mastiff was thrust inside, and the door was slammed shut. White Fang had never seen such a huge dog before, but he was not scared.
Here was something living, made of flesh—not wood or iron—that he could attack!
He leaped toward the mastiff, and with a flash of fangs, he ripped down the side of the mastiff's neck.
The mastiff shook his head, growled hoarsely, and lunged at White Fang. But the wolf was too fast. He leaped to the side and struck again.
He slashed with his fangs, and then leaped away, avoiding any attempt at a counterattack.
The men outside shouted and applauded, while Beauty grinned at White Fang's ferocious attack.
"There's no hope for the mastiff!" Beauty called gleefully. "That dog is too big and slow!"
In the end, while Beauty beat White Fang back with a club, the owner dragged out the dead mastiff.
There was a payment of bets, and money dropped into Beauty's hand.
Beauty laughed. "This wolf will make me rich!"
After that, there were more fights. White Fang began to enjoy the times when men gathered around his pen.
Locked up and separated from other living things, White Fang could satisfy his desire to cause harm and kill during these fights.
White Fang won more and more fights, and Beauty made lots of money. The wolf became well-known around Fort Yukon as a vicious fighter.
As his fame grew, the fights became more challenging.
One day White Fang was made to fight three dogs, one after the other. Each time he killed one dog, another dog was pushed into the pen.
Another day Beauty opened the pen, and someone pushed in a wolf, which had just been captured from the wild.
White Fang finished the animal off quickly. But then there was a day when two dogs were set on White Fang at once.
Though he managed to kill both of them, he was nearly killed in the process.
In the fall of that year, when the first snow was falling, Beauty boarded a steamer with White Fang and headed upriver to Dawson City, in the Klondike territory.
By now White Fang had acquired quite a reputation.
He was known as "the Fighting Wolf," and his cage on the steamer's deck was usually surrounded by curious men.
They stared at him, poked sticks between the bars to make him snarl, and then laughed at him.
Life for White Fang had become horrible. He raged at the men and showed them his teeth, or he lay quietly and studied them with cold hatred.
As a wild animal, White Fang was not meant to be held captive in such a confined space.
His captivity and terrible treatment at the hands of Beauty were transforming the wolf into something much more ferocious than nature had intended.
Weaker animals might have died from such a life, but White Fang endured.
In the past White Fang had known to cower down and submit to a man holding a club, but this wisdom had left the wolf.
The mere sight of Beauty Smith filled the wolf with rage. White Fang used to fall silent after being beaten.
Now, regardless of how terrible the beating was, he remained defiant.
It didn't matter how hard Beauty hit, or for how long; White Fang continued to growl and show his teeth.
And when Beauty finally walked away, the wolf sprang at the bars of his cage, snapping and snarling still.
When the steamer arrived in Dawson City, Beauty exhibited White Fang as "the Fighting Wolf."
Men paid fifty cents to see the wolf, and White Fang was given no rest. If he lay down to sleep, he was prodded with a sharp stick.
"Wake up!" Beauty shouted. "These people paid money to see you snarl!"
Whenever a fight could be arranged, Beauty took White Fang out of his cage and led him into the woods outside of town.
In order to avoid the police, this usually occurred at night. The audience arrived in the morning, along with White Fang's opponent.
The wolf fought dogs of all sizes, and most of these battles were to the death.
Not White Fang's death, of course, but that of any poor dog pitted against him. His method of fighting was based on quickness and surprise.
When the other dogs showed their fangs and started to threaten him, White Fang struck with lightning speed.
Over time White Fang's fights grew rarer. Most men became unwilling to pit their dogs against the legendary "Fighting Wolf," who was sure to win.
Beauty began pitting more wolves against White Fang, and then one day, a full-grown female lynx.
Fangs and claws slashed at the wolf, who fought desperately just to stay alive. And in the end, he did.
After that, all fighting ceased for White Fang.
There were no more animals with which to fight—at least there weren't any who stood a chance against him.
So the wolf remained on exhibition until spring, when a man named Tim Keenan arrived in Dawson City.
With him was a bulldog, the first of its kind to ever step foot in the Klondike.
As soon as this bulldog arrived, people began waiting for the day when it would fight White Fang.
At last the day arrived for White Fang to fight the bulldog.
Beauty Smith slipped the chain from White Fang's neck and stepped back.
The wolf stood inside the circle of men and studied the strange animal that faced him.
The dog was short and squat, with a large head. White Fang had never seen such a dog before.
Tim Keenan shoved the bulldog forward. "Go to it, Cherokee."
The dog waddled a few steps and then came to a stop. He blinked at White Fang.
"Attack him, Cherokee!" a man yelled.
"Eat him up!" another shouted.
Cherokee wagged his stumpy tail. Tim stepped into the circle and roughed up the bulldog.
Soon a low growl rose from the dog's throat. Tim shoved him forward and moved back.
Angry now, Cherokee broke into a swift, bow-legged run toward White Fang.
The wolf leaped forward in a flash, slashing the bulldog's neck and then springing away. The crowd roared.
Calmly, Cherokee moved toward the wolf again. White Fang leaped in with another attack—and another.
He darted left and right, slashing and biting.
Time went by. And while the wolf was all speed, the bulldog was pure determination.
Cherokee's ear was torn, and blood dripped from his neck; still, he kept fighting.
White Fang tried desperately to strike at Cherokee's throat, but the bulldog's low stature and wide jaw prevented such an attack.
Then something happened. White Fang had circled around Cherokee.
For a brief moment, the bulldog's head was turned away, leaving his shoulder exposed.
Here was a chance to knock the dog off his feet.
White Fang drove in upon Cherokee's shoulder, but his own shoulder was much higher.
He tumbled over the bulldog's body, and for the first time in his fighting career, White Fang lost his footing.
In an instant Cherokee's jaws clamped onto White Fang's throat. Shouts rose from the crowd.
White Fang tore around wildly. But he couldn't shake off the heavy body that hung from his throat.
The energy drained from the wolf, and he fell to his side. He craned his neck, searching for some part of the bulldog to bite.
His fangs snapped together with a sharp, empty click. Cherokee shifted his grip, and White Fang felt his airway squeeze shut.
It was at this time that a team of sled dogs came down the creek.
A man with a thick mustache drove the sled, and with him was a tall, young man.
Seeing the crowd, they stopped their dogs and came over to see what was happening.
By now White Fang had stopped struggling. Beauty entered the circle and kicked him savagely.
Beauty was getting ready to deliver another kick when a fist smashed into his face.
Beauty's whole body was lifted into the air before it crashed down in the snow.
The tall man stood in the circle, fists clenched, glaring furiously at the crowd. "You cowards!" he cried. "You beasts!"
He turned to the sled driver, the man with the mustache. "Come on, Matt. Lend a hand."
Matt entered the circle, and both men bent over the dogs.
The tall man yanked on Cherokee's jaw, muttering, "Beasts!" with each breath. But the bulldog's jaw was too strong to pry open.
The crowd began to yell at the two men who had ruined the day's entertainment. The tall man looked up from his work and glared again at them.
Matt was examining White Fang's throat. "The wolf isn't bleeding much, Weedon," he said. "I don't think the bite is very deep."
"It's not deep yet," Weedon replied grimly. He turned to the crowd. "Won't any of you help?"
Instead the crowd jeered at the newcomers, shouting out sarcastic advice.
"We need something to pry open that dog's mouth," Matt said.
Weedon pulled out his revolver, and worked its muzzle between the bulldog's jaws. The steel grated against the dog's teeth.
Tim stomped over. "Don't you dare break those teeth, stranger!"
Weedon looked up and asked, "Is he your dog?"
Tim grunted.
"Then get in here and break this grip."
"I can't," Tim said irritably. "I don't know how."
"Then don't bother me," Weedon snapped back. "I'm busy."
Finally Weedon managed to work the gun's barrel out through the other side of the bulldog's mouth.
Grabbing the barrel in one hand, and the gun's grip in the other, he pulled up, forcing Cherokee's jaw to open wider.
He glanced up at Tim. "Get ready to receive your dog."
Weedon gave one final pry. "Now!"
The dogs were pulled apart. The bulldog struggled vigorously.
"Take him away!" Weedon commanded, and Tim dragged Cherokee back into the crowd.
White Fang tried to get up, but he was too weak. He sank back down into the snow. His eyes were half-closed, and his mouth hung open.
Matt examined him. "He's nearly dead," he announced. "But he's still breathing."
Beauty came over. "I own that dog," he muttered.
Weedon glanced at the sled driver. "Matt, how much is a good sled dog worth?" he asked.
"Three hundred dollars," Matt replied.
"And how much for one that's half-dead?"
"Half of that."
Weedon turned to Beauty. "Did you hear that? I'm taking your dog from you, and I'm going to pay you 150 dollars for him." He counted out some bills.
"I'm not selling White Fang," said Beauty.
"Oh, yes you are," Weedon assured him. "Here's your money. The dog's mine now."
Beauty backed away and refused to take the money. Weedon clenched a fist.
Beauty looked down. "A man's got rights," he whimpered.
"You're right," Weedon said. "But you're not a man. You're a beast."
He shoved the money into Beauty's hand.
"Wait till I get back to Dawson City," Beauty threatened. "I'll tell the police."
Weedon narrowed his eyes. "If you do that, I'll have you run out of town. Understand?"
Beauty replied with a grunt.
"Yes or no?" Weedon demanded. "Do you understand?"
"Yes," Beauty replied meekly.
"Look out, Beauty!" someone in the crowd shouted. "That guy might bite you!"
A roar of laughter went up among the crowd.
As Weedon and Matt tended to White Fang, the crowd dispersed. Tim walked with a few other men.
He nodded back toward Weedon. "Who is that guy?" he asked.
"Weedon Scott," someone answered.
"And who is Weedon Scott?" Tim asked.
"He's a mining expert," the man said. "He's friends with all the big shots, including the gold commissioner.
If you want to keep out of trouble, you'll steer clear of him."
"I figured he was somebody important," Tim said. "That's why I didn't knock him out."
"It's hopeless," Weedon Scott said.
He sat on a step in front of his cabin and stared at Matt, who responded with a wry smile.
White Fang's chain was stretched taut. The two men watched as the wolf snarled at the sled dogs that lay nearby.
"That dog's a wolf and there's no taming him," Weedon said.
"Oh, I don't know about that, Weedon," Matt said. "There might be a lot of dog in White Fang. He's definitely been tamed already."
"No!"
"He's even been harnessed before," Matt added. "See those marks across his chest?"
"You're right," Weedon said. "He must have been a sled dog before Beauty Smith got hold of him."
Matt nodded. "There's no reason why he can't be a sled dog again."
"I suppose you're right again," Weedon said. Then his shoulders slumped, and the hopeful look in his eyes faded.
"We've had him two weeks, though, and he's still acting like a wild animal."
"Give him a chance," Matt suggested. "Let's take off that chain and let him roam around a bit."
Matt picked up a club and went over to White Fang. The wolf watched the club with keen eyes.
"See him keep his eyes on the club?" Matt said. "That's a good sign. He's no fool. He won't dare attack me as long as I'm holding it."
As Matt's hand approached White Fang's neck, the wolf crouched down, snarling and bristling.
His eyes darted back and forth between the club and the hand suspended threateningly above his head.
Matt unsnapped the chain from the collar and stepped back.
"Won't he run away?" Weedon asked.
Matt shrugged. "We'll find out."
At first White Fang could hardly believe he was free.
He walked with careful steps, his senses alert for any assault these two new gods might make against him.
After wandering past the corner of the cabin, he turned around and regarded the two gods intently.
"Poor devil," Weedon murmured. "What he needs is some show of human kindness." He went up the steps and into the cabin.
He came out with a piece of meat, which he tossed to White Fang. The wolf sprang away from the meat and then studied it suspiciously.
"Major, no!" Matt shouted.
One of the sled dogs dashed toward the meat. White Fang struck. Matt rushed in, but he was not quick enough.
The snow beneath Major reddened with blood.
Weedon shook his head. "It's too bad, but it served Major right."
Matt's foot swung down, on its way to kick White Fang. There was a leap and a flash of teeth, followed by a sharp exclamation from Matt.
"The wolf got me all right," Matt announced, pointing to his torn trousers and the growing stain of red.
"I told you it was hopeless," Weedon said. "I hate to say it, but there's just one thing to do."
As he talked, his hand pulled his revolver from its holster.
"Look here, Weedon," Matt said. "That dog has been treated terribly. You can't expect him to act like an angel all of a sudden. Give him some time."
"Look at Major," Weedon said.
Matt looked at the stricken dog. "It served him right. You said so yourself. He tried to take White Fang's meat, and now he's dead.
White Fang's not to blame. A dog who won't fight for his own meat isn't worth anything."
"But look at your leg," Weedon said.
Matt let out a hollow laugh. "If White Fang didn't do anything wrong, then I had no right to kick him."
Weedon shook his head. "He's untamable. It would be a mercy to kill him."
"Give the poor dog a chance," Matt said. "He's been through a terrible ordeal, and this is the first time he's been loose." He paused.
"I'll tell you what: if we can't tame him, I'll shoot him myself. I give you my word."
Weedon hesitated for another second and then tucked the revolver away.
"God knows I don't want to kill him or have him killed. Let's see what some kindness can do for him."
He walked over to White Fang and began talking to him gently and soothingly.
"Better have a club handy," Matt warned.
Weedon shook his head and went on speaking quietly to the wolf.
White Fang was suspicious. He didn't know what might happen. He had killed this god's dog and then bitten the other god.
Surely a terrible punishment awaited him. White Fang bristled and showed his teeth, prepared for anything. The god's hand was now reaching out.
White Fang crouched under it. He snarled, crouched lower, and still the hand descended.
Weedon had assumed he'd be quick enough to avoid getting bitten.
But he was not prepared for the remarkable speed of White Fang, who struck with the certainty and swiftness of a coiled snake.
Weedon cried out with surprise and held his torn hand tightly against his body. Matt disappeared into the cabin.
White Fang backed away, bristling and showing his fangs, his eyes full of menace.
He'd bitten two gods now. His punishment would be horrible—worse than any he'd suffered from the hands of Beauty.
"What are you doing?" Weedon cried suddenly.
Matt had come back out of the cabin with a rifle.
"I'm keeping the promise I made," Matt said.
"Don't do it!" Weedon cried.
"It needs to be done, Weedon."
"You said we should give him a chance," Weedon said. "Well, give it to him. We've only just started.
It served me right, getting so close to him so soon, and—look at him!"
White Fang was just past the corner of the cabin, snarling with blood-curdling viciousness. His eyes were fixed directly on the rifle in Matt's hands.
"He knows what a gun is!" Matt said.
"He's intelligent," Weedon said, "and we should give that intelligence a chance. Put the gun down."
Matt leaned the rifle against the woodpile. "Look at that!" he exclaimed. "The dog stopped snarling!"
Matt moved his hand toward the rifle again, and again angry snarls rose from White Fang's throat. When Matt drew back his hand, the snarling stopped.
"I'm going to try something," Matt whispered. "Don't worry—I won't shoot him."
Matt brought the rifle slowly to his shoulder. Right away the snarls resumed.
Just before the rifle came level to White Fang, the wolf leaped sidewise behind the corner of the cabin.
Looking through the scope, Matt saw only an empty space of snow. He put the rifle down.
"I agree with you, Weedon. That dog's too intelligent to kill."
White Fang snarled as Weedon Scott approached. It had been 24 hours since the wolf slashed open Weedon's hand.
White Fang expected a punishment and was prepared to fight back. But as the god stepped closer, he did something unexpected: he sat down.
In this position the god hardly seemed threatening, so White Fang's snarls grew quiet. Soon there was silence.
Weedon spoke, quietly and softly. The hair on White Fang's neck rose, and a vicious growl rushed up in his throat.
Weedon's calm voice mingled with the growls of the wolf, and the two sounds formed a sort of harmony in the cold winter air.
But even as White Fang bared his teeth, a feeling of security swept over him. No god had ever spoken kindly to him before.
After a long time, the god went into the cabin.
He came back out a moment later, sat down, and held out a small piece of meat.
The wolf inspected the meat with suspicion. Was this a trick?
Weedon tossed the meat into the snow. Keeping his eyes set firmly on the god, White Fang sniffed the meat and then ate it.
Another piece was held out. And again the hand tossed it into the snow.
When the god held out a third piece of meat, he did not toss it. He held it in front of White Fang's nose.
White Fang approached the hand, a low growl rumbling in his throat as a warning to the god. The wolf ate the meat, his eyes locked on Weedon's.
Weedon held out another piece, and the wolf ate that too. Soon the meat was gone.
White Fang licked his chops and waited to see what this strange god might do next. The god talked some more.
And then the hand approached again. White Fang snarled, the hair on his neck rising. His instinct told him to lash out, to attack.
But another part of him felt assured by the kindness in the man's voice. He crouched low as the hand came down.
When the hand touched him gently on the head, the wolf growled, but he did not attack.
He felt the hand lift up and come back down, patting him lightly. Then it moved behind his ears and began to rub. Here was a hand that did not give hurt.
"Unbelievable!" Matt cried when he came out of the cabin and saw his boss petting the wolf.
White Fang sprang backward and snarled viciously at Matt.
"You're liable to get yourself killed, Mr. Scott!" Matt said.
Weedon smiled and got up.
He walked over to the wolf, spoke quietly, and once again patted him on the head.
Matt chuckled. "I believe you missed your calling. You should have joined the circus as an animal tamer!"
White Fang grew to like his new god. With the exception of Kiche, no creature had ever shown the wolf kindness before.
Every day Weedon made time to sit down and pet him for a long while.
A low growl rumbled from within the wolf, but it wasn't an angry growl; it was one of satisfaction.
White Fang's feelings for Weedon deepened over time until the wolf didn't merely like the god—he loved him.
Each day White Fang waited eagerly for his master's return. And at night, while the other dogs slept, the wolf stood guard over the cabin.
One night a friend of Weedon's visited. White Fang leaped from the shadows, snapping and growling.
The man fought the wolf off with a club until Weedon came to the rescue.
The wolf soon learned the difference between honest men—friends of his god—and thieves. Honest men walked confidently up to the cabin door.
But if White Fang spotted a man sneaking through the woods, attempting to approach the cabin unseen, the wolf attacked without hesitation.
Killing his god's dogs was not allowed; White Fang knew that. He thrashed each and every one of them, though, to establish his superiority.
After that, he left them alone. When he walked among the dogs, they moved out of his way.
In a similar way, the wolf tolerated Matt. He saw the sled driver as another of Weedon's possessions—something to be protected.
White Fang proved himself a strong sled dog, and refused to be anything other than the team leader.
The other dogs obeyed him and feared him, and the men noticed that White Fang continued working at night, faithfully guarding his master's property.
"I'll tell you something, Mr. Scott," Matt said. "That wolf is worth a lot more than the $150 you paid Beauty Smith."
At the sound of Beauty's name, Weedon grimaced. "The beast!"
It was in late spring when White Fang's god abruptly disappeared.
Before the disappearance, bags had been packed, but the wolf hadn't known the meaning of that.
The wolf sat near the cabin's stoop one evening, waiting for his master's return.
By midnight the cold wind forced him to retreat to the rear of the cabin, where he tried to sleep.
His anxiety was too great, though. A couple of hours later, he was back near the stoop.
In the morning Matt came outside, and White Fang looked at him wistfully.
Of course, Matt had no way to tell the wolf that Weedon was away on a trip.
Days went by, and White Fang grew more and more miserable. He ate almost nothing, and let the other dogs thrash him.
Worried about the wolf's health, Matt brought him into the cabin to lie by the fire.
Down in Circle City, Weedon Scott received a letter from Matt. Most of the letter was related to business.
But at the end, Matt had written: The wolf won't work, and he won't eat. He's lost all his energy.
He wants to know what has become of you, and I don't know how to tell him. I'm afraid he might die.
White Fang's depression worsened. Then one night, as Matt read quietly, White Fang climbed to his feet and cocked his ears.
Footsteps! The door opened, and Weedon stepped in. The two men shook hands, and then Weedon asked, "Where's the wolf?"
White Fang stood near the fire, waiting.
"Holy smoke!" Matt said. "Look at him—he's wagging his tail!"
Weedon called his name, and the wolf trotted over. Weedon squatted down, face-to-face with White Fang, and rubbed the wolf's ears and neck.
Growling softly, the wolf pushed his head forward and nuzzled it deeply between Weedon's arm and body.
The two men looked at each other. Weedon's eyes were shining.
Weedon and Matt sat playing cards late one night. A shriek, accompanied by vicious snarling, caused the men to jump to their feet.
"The wolf's attacked somebody," Matt said.
"Bring a light!" Weedon shouted as he rushed outside.
Matt followed with the lamp, and by its light, they saw a man lying on his back. His arms were folded across his face and neck.
White Fang was in a rage, wickedly snapping, trying to get at the man's throat.
The sleeves of his flannel shirt were shredded, and blood streamed into the snow.
Weedon dragged White Fang away. "Quiet, boy!"
As Matt helped the man to his feet, the hideous face of Beauty Smith was revealed.
Beauty blinked in the lamplight and then caught sight of White Fang. A look of terror fell over the man's face.
Matt noticed two objects lying in the snow—a length of chain and a club. He held the lamp close so Weedon could see them.
Weedon looked at Matt and nodded. Then Matt laid his hand on Beauty's shoulder, turned him around, and shoved him back toward town.
White Fang growled softly as Weedon petted him.
"Tried to steal you, huh?" Weedon said. "And you wouldn't allow that! Well, he made a mistake, didn't he?"
Matt chuckled in agreement.
Time went by, and White Fang began to sense a change in Weedon.
Through careful observation of his god, the wolf could tell that a big event was going to take place.
"I believe the wolf's on to you, Mr. Scott," Matt said one evening at supper.
Outside they could hear White Fang whining and sniffing at the bottom of the cabin door.
Weedon sighed. "What can I possibly do with a wolf in California?"
"That's a good question," Matt replied.
"He'd kill dogs on sight," Weedon went on. "I'd wind up getting sued and going bankrupt.
Or worse—the authorities would take him away from me and put him down."
"He's a downright murderer, I know," Matt said.
Weedon looked at Matt for a moment. "It would never do, Matt. He can't come with me."
"I agree," Matt said.
"Then that settles it."
The two men sat quietly. Outside, White Fang continued to whine.
"There's no denying he loves you," Matt said.
"I know that." Weedon paused for a minute. "But it would be crazy for me to take him with me."
"That's true," Matt said. He glanced over at the cabin door. "How does he know you're leaving anyway?"
Weedon shook his head. "I have no idea."
A few days later, White Fang spied Weedon's luggage through the cabin's open door.
That night White Fang sat near the stoop of the cabin, pointed his nose to the stars, and let out a long and sad howl.
Inside the cabin the two men had just gone to bed.
"He stopped eating today," Matt remarked from his bunk.
There was a grunt from Weedon's bunk, and a stir of blankets.
"Considering how he was the last time you went away," Matt said, "I wouldn't be surprised if he died this time."
"Oh, shut up!" Weedon cried out through the darkness. "I can't take him with me!"
"I know, I know."
The next day White Fang whined as Weedon packed his clothes into canvas bags.
Matt rolled blankets and furs inside a small tarpaulin. Later two Indians arrived and picked up the luggage.
Matt led them down the hill, into town, and returned a short while later. Weedon came to the cabin door and called White Fang inside.
"You poor devil," he said, gently rubbing behind White Fang's ears.
"I'm hitting the long trail, where you cannot follow. Now give me a growl—a really good, good-bye growl."
But White Fang refused. After a wistful, searching look at Weedon, he snuggled in, burrowing his head out of sight between his master's arm and body.
"There's the whistle!" Matt cried. "The steamship's about to set sail. Lock the front door, Mr. Scott. I'll go out the back."
The two doors slammed at the same moment, leaving White Fang locked inside.
Weedon waited for Matt to come around to the front. From inside the door came a low whining.
"Take good care of him," Weedon said, as they walked down the hill. "Write and let me know how he's doing."
"Sure," Matt answered. "But listen to that, will you?"
Both men stopped. White Fang was howling as dogs howl when their masters lie dead.
It was the saddest howl the men had ever heard—filled with heartbreaking grief.
The steamship's deck was crowded with gold-seekers, all eager to leave the Klondike and return home.
Matt and Weedon were shaking hands when Matt's gaze fixed on something behind Weedon.
The other turned around to see. Sitting on the deck several feet away was White Fang.
"Did you lock the front door?" Matt asked.
Weedon nodded. "How about the back door?"
"You bet I did," Matt replied.
White Fang watched Weedon intently.
Matt sighed. "I'll have to take him ashore with me."
Matt took a few steps toward White Fang, but the wolf sprang away. Matt sprinted, and White Fang dodged between the legs of a group of men.
Ducking and turning, he shot around the deck, eluding Matt's efforts to capture him.
"White Fang, here!" Weedon commanded.
The wolf trotted immediately to his god.
Weedon ran his hands through White Fang's fur and then bent closer.
"Look at that, Matt," he said. "He's got fresh cuts on his muzzle, and there's a gash between his eyes."
Matt passed his hand along White Fang's belly.
"He's all cut up," Matt said. "He must have jumped through the window!"
The steamship's whistle sounded. All around, "good-byes" were said and some people headed back down the gangplank to the dock. Matt reached for White Fang.
Weedon grasped the other man's hand. "Good-bye, Matt. About the wolf—you don't have to write. You see, I'm going to . . ."
"What!" Matt exclaimed.
Weedon nodded. "I'll write to you about him."
Matt headed down the gangplank. Halfway down, he shouted back at Weedon, "He'll never stand the climate! You'll have to clip him in warm weather!"
As the steamship moved away from the dock, Weedon waved a last good-bye to Matt. Then he bent over White Fang and rubbed behind the wolf's ears.
"Now growl for me!"
White Fang and Weedon got off the steamship in San Francisco. Instead of log cabins or tepees, towering buildings rose toward the sky.
Everywhere the wolf looked, new dangers seemed to threaten him: automobiles, horse-drawn carts, and cable cars.
As Weedon strode through the bustling crowds, the wolf followed close behind, never letting the god escape his sight.
Weedon led the wolf into the baggage car of a train, chained him in a corner, and then left. Other gods brought in luggage and tossed it into piles.
At first White Fang thought he'd been deserted by his master. But then he caught a familiar scent.
Lying next to him were the canvas bags filled with his master's clothes. Reassured, the wolf sat down and guarded the bags.
An hour later the door opened. Weedon unchained White Fang, and the wolf stepped out to find that the city was gone.
Before him was a quiet landscape, streaming with sunshine. A horse-drawn carriage waited nearby.
The master's bags were placed inside. Then a man and a woman approached. The woman's arms went out and clutched Weedon—a hostile act!
The next moment Weedon had torn loose from the embrace and grabbed White Fang, who was snarling furiously.
"It's all right, Mother," Weedon said. "He thought you were going to injure me, and he wouldn't stand for it. He'll learn soon enough."
"And in the meantime, I can love my son when his dog is not around." She laughed, though she looked frightened.
White Fang continued to snarl, his eyes fixed on Weedon's mother.
"No, Mother," Weedon said. "He'll have to learn, and he shall do so right now."
He spoke softly to White Fang until the wolf calmed down.
Then his voice became firm. "Down, sir! Down with you!"
White Fang lay down, though he did so reluctantly.
"Now, Mother." Weedon opened his arms for an embrace, but he kept his eyes on White Fang.
Weedon's mother stepped forward. The hair on White Fang's neck bristled, and he made a slight move.
"Down!" Weedon commanded.
White Fang sank back and watched as the woman put her arms around his master.
No harm came from it, so the wolf relaxed. When the strange man-god embraced Weedon, no harm came from that either.
The three gods climbed into the carriage, and the driver signaled the horses to start.
White Fang ran alongside the horses, his hair bristling, warning them not to harm his master.
After 15 minutes the carriage turned in through a stone gateway and drove down a lane lined with walnut trees.
Green lawns stretched out on either side, their surface broken here and there by mighty oaks.
In the distance hay fields showed tan and gold, and beyond them were rolling hills of pasture. The carriage headed toward a large house with many windows and a deep porch.
Just then a sheepdog ran in front of White Fang, preventing him from following the carriage.
The wolf made a silent and deadly rush toward the dog. The rush, however, was never completed.
The wolf's legs went stiff, and he skidded to a stop. The sheepdog was a female, and instinct demanded that he not attack her.
The female had no such instinct. She was a sheepdog, bred to protect sheep, and here was a wolf!
She sprang upon White Fang and bit deep. The wolf backed away, trying to spy a way around her. He dodged to the left and the right.
But regardless of where he tried to go, the sheepdog remained between him and the carriage.
White Fang sprinted across the lawn, running in a wide circle. But again the sheepdog placed herself in front of him.
The carriage continued to carry the master farther away. White Fang saw it disappear behind some trees.
The situation was desperate. The wolf charged at the sheepdog, hitting her squarely on the shoulder.
She rolled off her feet, and seeing his chance for escape, the wolf tore down the path.
The sheepdog sprinted after him. But now that White Fang was running in a straight line, she had no hope of catching him.
Silent as a ghost, the wolf glided swiftly over the ground. He rounded the house and saw his master getting out of the carriage.
Then something struck White Fang from the side, and the wolf was hurled to the ground.
He clambered back to his feet, his ears flattened and lips drawn back, and saw another large dog—a deerhound.
White Fang leaped in for the hound's throat. But just before his fangs reached their target, the sheepdog swept in. Again the wolf was knocked off his feet.
The next moment the master arrived. He held White Fang as his father called off the two dogs.
"I say, this is a fine reception for a poor lone wolf from the Arctic," Weedon remarked. White Fang calmed down under his caressing hand.
"I heard that he's only been knocked off his feet once before. Now it's happened twice in thirty seconds!"
Other strange gods came out of the house.
A woman threw her arms around the master. White Fang had now learned to tolerate this act.
But when one of the gods reached out to touch White Fang, the wolf warned her off with a snarl. The master quickly explained.
Weedon's father led the hound up onto the porch. "Dick!" he commanded. "Lie down."
The hound obeyed, but from his spot on the porch, he continued to growl and watch the wolf.
The sheepdog was growling too.
One of the women caressed her. "You're not being very friendly, Collie."
"Come, let's go inside," Weedon's father said.
The other gods started up the porch steps. White Fang followed closely at Weedon's heels. Dick growled, and the wolf growled back.
"Let's take Collie inside and let those two fight it out," Weedon's father suggested. "After that, they'll be friends."
Weedon laughed. "Friends, you say? White Fang will be the chief mourner at Dick's funeral."
Weedon's father looked nervously at the wolf. "Do you mean . . .?"
Weedon nodded. "I sure do. Dick would be dead within a minute. Maybe two." He turned to White Fang. "Come on, you wolf. It's you who has to come inside."
White Fang walked up the steps and across the porch, keeping his eyes on Dick.
The wolf entered the house and sniffed around until he was convinced it didn't hold any new threats. Then he trotted over to his master and lay down.
Still, he stayed alert, ready to spring instantly to his feet.
White Fang soon felt comfortable in his new home in California. The estate was called Sierra Vista, and it belonged to Weedon's father, Judge Scott.
The deerhound, Dick, quickly learned that White Fang wasn't a threat. The hound made friendly advances toward the wolf.
But White Fang snarled, and after that the hound left him alone.
White Fang had been an enemy to other dogs for his entire life; it was too late for him to change now.
The sheepdog, Collie, continued to distrust the wolf. She harassed and bullied him constantly.
White Fang's instincts still wouldn't let him fight back against the female, so he was forced to either tolerate her attacks or retreat.
The wolf discovered that many people in this new domain were important to his master.
To the wolf they were the master's possessions, things to be protected.
There was Judge Scott and his wife, along with the master's two sisters.
There was also the master's wife, Alice, and their two young children, Weedon and Maud.
White Fang growled when the children first approached him. But a sharp word from the master silenced the wolf.
He bristled as the children's tiny hands moved across his body, yet he tolerated their caresses.
From then on the wolf allowed the master's children to approach whenever they wanted to, and he soon grew to enjoy their company.
One day the wolf sauntered around the corner of the house and came upon a chicken that had escaped from one of the chicken yards.
In an instant there was a flash of teeth and a frightened squawk. White Fang licked his chops. The chicken had been fat and tender—a very good meal.
Later that day he found another stray chicken near the stables.
When White Fang prepared to attack, a worker grabbed a whip and lashed at the wolf. Without a sound White Fang leaped for the man's throat.
"Oh no!" The man stumbled backward, raising his arms to protect his throat. His forearm was ripped open to the bone.
Just then Collie rushed upon White Fang, barking and snapping. As the man retreated into the stable, White Fang fled from the angry dog.
Moments later Weedon heard what had happened.
"I'll teach him to leave the chickens alone," Weedon told the worker. "But I can't do that until I catch him in the act."
For two days White Fang observed the chicken yards. Then one night he climbed to the top of a pile of lumber.
From there he leaped onto the roof of a chicken house and dropped down into the yard. By the morning fifty hens lay dead.
Weedon looked at White Fang, and his lips tightened. He knew what he had to do, though he did not want to.
He spoke harshly to White Fang, holding the wolf's nose down to one of the slain hens and cuffing him.
White Fang realized he had committed a crime. He had destroyed his master's property, and now his master was furious.
In the North, where White Fang had grown up, any animal could be hunted and eaten.
But here in the South, things were apparently different. The gods owned certain animals, and those animals must be left alone.
The master led White Fang into one of the chicken yards. When the wolf saw the plump birds pecking at the ground, his instinct was to pounce.
"No," Weedon commanded.
Forcing himself to ignore his instinct, the wolf obeyed his god.
Weedon practiced this routine with White Fang several more times, until he was sure the lesson had been learned.
"You can never cure a chicken-killer," Judge Scott said at lunch one day. "Once it's got the taste of blood . . ." He shook his head sadly.
"I'll tell you what I'll do," Weedon said. "I'll lock White Fang in with some chickens all afternoon."
His father raised an eyebrow. "But—"
"And for every chicken he kills," Weedon went on, "I'll pay you one dollar."
"And what if Father loses the bet?" Weedon's sister, Beth, asked. "What will he have to do?"
Everyone at the table looked at Weedon.
Weedon pondered the issue for a moment.
"All right, Father. For every ten minutes that White Fang remains in the chicken yard without harming chickens, you must say to him, 'White Fang, you are smarter than I thought.'"
The judge agreed, so after lunch Weedon locked White Fang in one of the chicken yards.
From various vantage points, the family members watched the wolf. White Fang slept for a couple of hours, waking up once to drink from the water trough.
He ignored the chickens entirely. Finally he jumped onto the roof of the chicken house, over the fence, and out of the chicken yard.
Later, on the porch everyone watched with delight as Judge Scott sat face-to-face with White Fang.
Sixteen times the judge pronounced slowly and solemnly, "White Fang, you are smarter than I thought."
White Fang became an expert at suppressing his killer instincts. He knew to leave the master's livestock alone.
And when walking through town behind his god, White Fang could easily ignore the large cuts of fresh meat hanging outside the butcher's shop.
People in town pointed at the wolf, and a few of them bravely placed their hands on his head. All of this White Fang tolerated.
A saloon sat alongside the road into town. In front of this saloon sat three dogs who'd made it a habit to rush at White Fang every time he walked by.
The wolf knew he must not fight, so he merely snarled at them and continued to walk.
One day, however, some men stood outside the saloon. As the dogs barked, the men laughed and encouraged them to attack.
Weedon stopped walking and looked at White Fang. "Go to it, wolf."
Confused, White Fang looked at his master and then at the barking dogs. He looked back at Weedon.
Weedon nodded. "Go ahead, old fellow. Eat them up!"
There was a great snarling and growling, a clashing of teeth, and a flurry of bodies.
The dust on the road arose in a cloud and screened the battle. After several minutes two dogs were struggling in the dirt and the third was running away.
The dog leaped a ditch, went through a rail fence, and fled across a field. White Fang raced after the dog, dragging him down in the middle of the field and slaying him.
Word about the fight spread across the valley, and from then on, people made sure their dogs stayed away from the Fighting Wolf.
The months went by, and White Fang lived a happy life in Sierra Vista.
Human kindness was like a sun shining upon him, and he flourished like a flower planted in good soil.
Collie, however, never gave the wolf a moment's peace. Weedon had encouraged her to be friends with White Fang, but she defied these efforts.
Instead she followed White Fang constantly.
If the wolf even glanced at a chicken, Collie snarled with indignation and wrath.
White Fang's favorite way of ignoring her was to lie down with his head on his front paws, and pretend to sleep. This always dumbfounded and silenced her.
White Fang had always hated the laughter of the gods. Being laughed at filled the wolf with rage.
But he could not be angry with Weedon, and when that god laughed at him in a good-natured way, the wolf was confused.
He felt anger rising in him, but his love for the master was stronger than his anger.
Not knowing how to react, White Fang sat up straight and made himself look dignified. Weedon laughed harder.
When the wolf tried to look even more dignified, Weedon laughed harder than before.
In the end the master laughed White Fang out of his dignity.
The wolf's jaws parted slightly, his lips lifted a little, and a quizzical expression came into his eyes. White Fang had learned to laugh.
Likewise he learned to romp with Weedon, to be tumbled down and rolled over.
In return, he pretended to be angry, growling ferociously, and snapping his teeth together.
But he was careful to never bite the master.
At the end of such a romp, Weedon and White Fang laughed. The master threw his arms around White Fang's neck while the wolf growled lovingly.
Weedon often went out on horseback, and White Fang accompanied him. No outing was too far or too strenuous for White Fang.
His was the gait of the wolf—smooth, tireless, and effortless. He'd run fifty miles and still arrive home ahead of the horse.
One day Weedon was attempting to open a gate without dismounting his horse.
But every time he approached the gate, the horse became frightened and reared up.
Weedon jabbed the animal with his spurs. The horse dropped its forelegs and then kicked wildly with its rear legs.
White Fang watched with increasing anxiety until he could contain himself no longer.
He sprang in front of the horse and, for the first time in his life, the wolf barked.
The horse bucked again, throwing Weedon off. The master slammed into the ground and broke his leg.
Furious at the horse, the wolf sprang. But Weedon's sharp voice stopped him.
"Home!" Weedon commanded. "Go home!"
White Fang refused to leave his master.
Weedon searched his pockets for pencil and paper, hoping to write a note for his family. But his pockets were empty. Again he commanded the wolf to run home.
White Fang regarded his master wistfully, trotted off a few steps, and then returned, whining softly.
Weedon spoke to him gently. "It's all right, old fellow. You just run along home," he said.
"Go on home and tell everyone what's happened to me. Home with you, you wolf. Go home!"
White Fang cocked his ears.
He knew the meaning of "home," and though he did not understand everything the master was saying, he understood the master wanted him to go there.
White Fang turned and trotted away reluctantly. Then he stopped and looked back over his shoulder.
"Go home!" Weedon commanded, and this time the wolf obeyed.
Weedon's family was on the porch when White Fang arrived. He bounded up the steps, panting and covered with dust.
"Weedon must be back," Weedon's mother announced.
The children welcomed White Fang with glad cries and ran to meet him.
The wolf avoided them and passed down the porch, but they cornered him against a rocking chair and the railing. He growled and tried to push by them.
Their mother bit her lip. "He makes me nervous around the children," she said. "I worry that he will turn upon them unexpectedly some day."
White Fang growled and sprang out of the corner, knocking over the two children.
"Come here, children," said their mother. "Leave White Fang alone."
"A wolf cannot be trusted!" Judge Scott said.
"Weedon believes White Fang is part dog, but he doesn't know for sure. Just look at his fur! It's clear that he's—"
He did not finish his sentence. White Fang leaped before him, growling fiercely.
"Go away! Lie down, sir!" Judge Scott commanded.
White Fang turned to Alice, the master's wife. She screamed as he seized the hem of her dress with his teeth and pulled, tearing the fabric.
The wolf let go, stopped his growling, and stood still. He looked at everyone.
He opened his mouth and worked his throat muscles, desperately trying to communicate with the confused gods.
"What is he doing?" Alice asked.
"I hope he is not going mad," said Weedon's mother.
"I believe he's trying to speak," Beth announced.
For the second time in his life, White Fang barked.
"I think something has happened to Weedon!" Alice exclaimed.
Everyone sprang up, and White Fang ran down the steps. He looked back for them to follow and barked once more.
With the family now hurrying after him, White Fang rushed back to his master.
After that event White Fang was loved more than ever by Weedon's family.
Judge Scott continued to distrust the wolf and often cited information about wolf behavior in the wild, but the others ignored the old man's arguments.
As White Fang's second winter in California approached, he made a strange discovery.
There was now a playfulness in Collie's bites; a certain gentleness prevented them from really hurting the wolf.
He quickly forgot the past torment she'd caused him, and was soon prancing about and playing with his former enemy.
One day Collie led White Fang on a long chase through the back pasture and toward the woods.
Weedon was planning to go horseback riding, and White Fang normally would have accompanied him. But there was now an instinct in the wolf that couldn't be ignored.
This instinct ran deeper than his need to obey the laws, deeper than his love for the master, even deeper than his own will to live.
Weedon rode alone that day, while deep in the woods, White Fang ran alongside Collie, just as his mother, Kiche, and old One Eye had run many years before in the silent North.
As White Fang enjoyed his life at Sierra Vista, newspapers carried the story of a ferocious man who'd escaped from prison. His name was Jim Hall.
Growing up in a San Francisco slum, Jim had lived a terrible life.
Society treated him cruelly, and he became a hardened criminal. Twice, he was locked up in prison, where he was beaten and starved.
After each prison stay, he returned to society even more vicious.
Perhaps some kindness would have benefited him. But society never offered him any kindness.
The third time Jim Hall was sentenced to prison, it was for life. There, he killed a prison guard who'd treated him unfairly.
Jim was placed in an iron cell with no windows. For three years he never saw the sky, the sunshine, or even a human face.
Guards slipped food through an opening in the door without saying a word.
The cell was an iron tomb, and Jim became wild, howling his fury at the cold walls.
And then one night, Jim escaped. The body of a dead guard lay in the doorway of the empty cell.
Two other guards lay dead in the yard, their guns stolen. Now Jim was armed and on the loose.
Police, accompanied by packs of bloodhounds, searched the countryside.
A large reward was offered to whoever captured the criminal; farmers and ranchers grabbed rifles and joined the hunt.
But the trail soon went cold, and Jim Hall seemed to have disappeared.
Weedon's family read the newspapers with anxiety. It was Judge Scott who had sentenced Jim Hall to life in prison.
The judge didn't know it, but Jim was innocent. Police had framed him for a crime he hadn't committed.
Standing in the courtroom, Jim had flown into a rage.
"You'll regret this, Judge Scott!" he shrieked as court officers dragged him from the room.
White Fang, of course, knew nothing of the convict's escape. But one night he awoke suddenly. His nose sensed a strange god in the house.
Hearing soft footsteps, he stood up and followed silently.
In the wild he'd hunted live meat that startled at the slightest sound; White Fang knew the advantage of surprise.
The strange god paused at the foot of the great staircase. White Fang's hair bristled.
Those stairs led up to where the master and his family were sleeping! As soon as the man placed a foot on the first step, White Fang struck.
Burying his fangs into the man's neck, the wolf dragged him to the floor.
Weedon and his family awoke in alarm as shots fired from a revolver. The sound of a man's screams mingled with snarls and growls from White Fang.
Furniture crashed, and glass shattered. And then there was silence.
Everyone huddled near the top of the staircase. Weedon pressed a button, and the house was flooded with light.
He and Judge Scott, revolvers in hand, tiptoed down the stairs. In the middle of the wreckage of smashed furniture, a man lay dead.
Judge Scott gasped. "Jim Hall!"
He and Weedon looked at each other, recognizing what might have happened.
Then they turned to White Fang. The wolf opened his eyes slightly as the two men bent over him.
His tail moved in an attempt to wag, and his throat rumbled a weak growl, which quickly ceased.
The wolf's eyelids drooped and went shut, and his whole body seemed to relax and flatten out upon the floor.
"Poor wolf," Weedon muttered. "Hall shot him. There's no way White Fang will live."
"We'll see about that!" Judge Scott rushed to the telephone.
A doctor arrived and tended to White Fang's wounds.
After an hour and a half, early morning light crept through the windows. The family gathered to hear the doctor's verdict.
Judge Scott wrung his hands. "Please tell us you have good news. This wolf saved my life."
The doctor shook his head. "I'm afraid he won't survive. He has a broken leg, three broken ribs, and he's lost a lot of blood.
He was shot three times. He likely has internal injuries that I can't see."
Though they had little hope he'd survive, the family cared for White Fang day and night, keeping him well-fed and comfortable.
Imprisoned in his bandages and plaster cast, the wolf clung to life.
He slept long hours, a parade of memories passing through his mind.
Once again he lived in the lair with Kiche, trembled before Gray Beaver, and ran for his life from Lip-lip and the snarling pack of puppies.
And again he relived his days with Beauty Smith, fighting to the death.
In the wild the weak perish quickly and only the strongest survive.
White Fang had suffered greatly in the wild, but that suffering had forged in him a strong body and spirit. Now that strength drove him to live.
Finally, after several weeks, the last bandage and the plaster cast came off. The family gathered around as Weedon rubbed White Fang behind the ears.
The wolf growled lovingly and tried to stand up. He'd lain for so long, though, his muscles had lost their strength.
After a few falls, he finally managed to totter on all four legs.
"No dog could do that," Judge Scott declared. "Only a wolf!"
"He'll have to learn to walk again," said the doctor, "so he might as well start right now. Let him go outside."
And outside White Fang went, like a king, with everyone following. He was very weak, and when he reached the lawn, he lay down and rested.
Then he stood back up and continued. Strength returned to his muscles as blood began to surge through them.
White Fang reached the stables and saw Collie, surrounded by six puppies playing in the sun.
She snarled a warning at the wolf, and he was careful to keep his distance.
Weedon nudged one puppy toward him. White Fang's hair bristled.
"It's okay, old boy," Weedon said.
Collie snarled at the wolf as one of Weedon's sisters held her back. White Fang cocked his ears and watched the puppy approach.
Their noses touched, and he felt the puppy's warm little tongue on his snout. Instinctively, White Fang's tongue went out and licked the puppy's face.
The gods clapped, and White Fang looked over with a puzzled expression. Then the other puppies began to clamber and tumble over him.
The gods laughed, and for a moment, the wolf felt self-conscious and awkward.
But these feelings quickly passed, replaced by a deep feeling of contentedness.
Surrounded by the tiny, soft bodies, White Fang closed his eyes and dozed in the warm sun.
